why: Ask a class how they revise and most will describe some version of reading their notes again. It feels productive, and that is the problem: the conditions that feel smooth and productive, rereading and massed practice, mostly produce confidence without retention.

Roediger and Karpicke showed that students who were tested on material remembered far more, weeks later, than students who restudied it for the same time. The card puts the implication plainly: the testing is the learning, not the preparation for it.
example: Before an end-of-topic check, an English class spends ten minutes not re-reading their anthology notes but writing what they remember about a poem's imagery, then checking against the notes. The time cost is the same as a read-through; what has changed is where the effort sits.
notice: How pupils react when the notes close. Reluctance to retrieve without them is often the illusion of knowing at work.
What the checking stage turns up. The gaps pupils find themselves are the ones re-reading would have hidden.
Whether confidence and recall match. Pupils who felt they knew the material from reading it may find they cannot produce it.
consider: This substitutes for re-reading rather than adding to it. The time pupils would have spent reviewing notes becomes the retrieval attempt plus the check.
Expect some resistance at first. Retrieval feels harder than reading, and the research suggests that difficulty is doing the useful work, not signalling a problem.
pages.wider: This is the testing effect at its most direct: Roediger and Karpicke found retrieval did more for retention weeks later than restudying, and Dunlosky's reviews rank practice testing among the most effective techniques available.

why: Five questions at the start of the lesson, on prior content, with nothing going in the gradebook. The routine is unremarkable to watch, which is rather the point: it makes regular retrieval a habit instead of an event.

The stakes are doing real work here. Agarwal found routine quizzing reduces test anxiety rather than causing it; when quizzing is frequent and nothing rides on it, it stops being a threat and becomes practice. As the card says, the quiz is not the assessment. It is the learning.
example: A science class starts every lesson the same way: five questions on the board covering earlier topics, answered from memory in the back of books, self-marked in a minute. Nothing is collected and nothing is graded. The teacher notes which questions caused trouble and moves on.
pages.try: Pick one class and run five questions tomorrow, self-marked. Reusing questions from earlier lessons is fine; frequency beats novelty.
notice: Which questions the class keeps getting wrong. Those topics need reteaching, not just re-quizzing.
Whether the routine stays low-stakes in feel as well as in fact. Agarwal's finding shows up as pupils treating the quiz as normal.
How long it actually takes. If the starter is swallowing fifteen minutes, trim the admin, not the retrieval.
consider: Keeping it out of the gradebook is not an optional nicety; the low stakes are what make the anxiety finding hold.
Self-marking keeps the workload at zero and puts the checking where it is most useful, in the pupil's hands, immediately.
tech: This is the routine where an approved quiz or response tool in your setting can genuinely help: quick two-minute starters every lesson with no marking, and results you can glance at while pupils move on. Let the tool manage the admin, the collecting and the scoring, and keep the retrieval effort with the pupils. If it starts to feel like a fastest finger first round, rewarding speed over thought, it is removing the difficulty that makes the practice worthwhile.

stair.lede: Writing five fresh questions every lesson is drafting work AI does well, through the approved tool in your setting. This is Mark's own STAIR example for exactly this job:
stair.prompt:
Act as a primary teacher who is a science specialist. Create retrieval questions on the water cycle for Year 5. Keep tightly to evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection. Present the output in clearly labelled sections.

Pupils should be able to demonstrate confident explanations and supply short applied questions.

Every question must include plausible distractors based on age-appropriate misconceptions.

Keep all questions concise with no added detail, definitions or answers.
stair.after: Swap the role, topic and year group for yours, then iterate until the questions match what you actually taught. That's the I in STAIR. The judgement about which questions make the cut stays with you.

pages.wider: Roediger and Karpicke supply the memory case for frequent testing; Agarwal's classroom studies supply the reassurance that, done routinely and without stakes, it reduces test anxiety rather than feeding it.

why: Most revision defaults to putting information back in front of pupils: re-reading, highlighting, copying notes. The research in this guide points the other way. Retrieval, getting knowledge out, does more for long term memory than another pass over the page.

A brain dump is the simplest possible version of that. It needs no preparation, no question writing and no technology, and it gives you something a quiz cannot: a picture of what pupils reach for unprompted, and in what order.
example: Two lessons into a new topic, a class gets a blank page and two minutes: write everything you remember about last lesson. No notes, no talking. Afterwards, pupils open their books and check what they missed. The teacher asks for one thing that did not come back, and the answers shape the start of the next lesson.
pages.try: End one lesson this week with it. Two minutes, blank page, everything you remember from today. Keep it out of any book you mark; the point is the retrieval, not the record.
notice: What most of the class could not recall. The card says it plainly: that is precisely where teaching needs to return.
Who writes steadily and who freezes at the blank page. Freezing is information too, and cued recall is a gentler step back.
Whether what comes back is what you would have predicted. It often is not.
consider: There has to be something to retrieve. If the material was only met once, a brain dump measures the teaching more than the pupils.
The imperfect attempt is the point, so resist tidying it into a marked task. The moment it carries stakes, pupils play safe and you lose the honest picture.
pages.wider: This sits squarely in the testing effect tradition: Roediger and Karpicke showed that the act of retrieving is itself a learning event, not just a measure of one.
tech: Paper does this job perfectly well. Where the approved shared document or whiteboard tool in your setting adds something is speed of reading: thirty attempts visible at once, skimmable for the gaps, without collecting a single book. The retrieval effort is the important part, not the admin around it.

why: Quizzing pupils on content they have not yet been taught sounds backwards, and that is exactly the card's claim: struggling to retrieve primes the brain, and students who fail before instruction remember the answer more reliably once taught.
It reframes failure as preparation. The wrong answers are not a problem to manage; they are the priming.
example: Before a lesson introducing the causes of the First World War, a history teacher poses three questions the class cannot yet answer well and asks for best guesses. No marks, no discussion beyond a brief reveal. The lesson then teaches the material, and the earlier guesses give the new content something to attach to.
pages.try: Open one new topic with two or three questions pupils cannot yet answer, asked for best guesses, before any teaching. Keep it brief; the priming is the point, not the score.
notice: How pupils handle being asked what they do not know. The activity only works if guessing wrong is visibly safe.
Whether the pre-tested material comes back more reliably later than material introduced without the quiz.
consider: Be explicit with the class about why you are doing it. Pupils told that failure here is productive respond differently from pupils who suspect they are being caught out.
This pairs naturally with the generation effect: a wrong answer generated before the right one is revealed is doing encoding work.
pages.wider: Bjork's work on pretesting and Kapur's on productive failure point the same way: unsuccessful retrieval before instruction can prepare memory for what follows.

why: Reconstruction sits between a brain dump and a formal test. Pupils rebuild the key ideas of a topic from memory, then open their notes and correct in a different colour. Karpicke and Blunt found this outperforms re-reading.
The second colour is what makes it more than a memory exercise. The corrections are the data: for the pupil, a precise record of what did not come back; for you, a page you can read at a glance.
example: At the end of a unit on rivers, pupils close their books and write out the processes of erosion from memory. Ten minutes later they open their notes and add what they missed in green pen. Flicking through the books afterwards, the teacher can see the same two processes missing in green across half the class.
pages.try: Run it once at the end of a current topic: reconstruct from memory, then correct in colour. The colour matters; without it the gaps disappear into the page.
notice: Where the second colour clusters. Whole-class gaps are a reteaching list, written by the pupils themselves.
Whether corrections are additions or fixes. Missing knowledge and mangled knowledge need different responses.
consider: Resist marking the reconstruction itself. The imperfect first attempt is the mechanism, and stakes push pupils back towards playing safe.
The check against notes is part of the learning, not an admin step; give it proper time.
pages.wider: Karpicke and Blunt found rebuilding from memory outperformed re-reading for retention, even though the re-reading felt more productive at the time; this is the testing effect applied to whole topics rather than single questions.

why: Ebbinghaus mapped the forgetting curve well over a century ago; Cepeda's work put numbers on the gaps that help most. The finding has not really changed: retrieval spread across days and weeks does more for retention than the same practice massed into one session.
The hard part is not believing it, it is timetabling it. Which is why the card aims this at your medium-term plan rather than your lesson plan: the calendar is part of the pedagogy.
example: Planning a six-week unit, a teacher pencils review points in before the content: week three revisits week one, week five revisits weeks two and three, and the following unit opens by retrieving this one. Nothing about any single lesson changes much; the shape of the term does.
pages.try: Take the medium-term plan for your next unit and mark two points where earlier content will come back. Booking the slots is the habit; the questions can be written later.
notice: What the first spaced review reveals. Material that seemed secure at the time will have faded; that is the forgetting curve, not a teaching failure.
Whether the review points survive contact with a busy term. If they are the first thing cut, they were never really planned in.
consider: Massed practice feels better in the room, for you and for pupils. Expect the spaced version to look worse lesson by lesson while doing more across the term.
tech: Spaced repetition tools exist for exactly this problem: they revisit older material at the right intervals automatically, which matches the research while saving you the headache of tracking it manually. If your setting has an approved one, let it carry the scheduling. The intervals are the tool's job; making sure what comes back is worth retrieving remains yours.
pages.wider: Cepeda and colleagues quantified the gaps Ebbinghaus first mapped, and Dunlosky's reviews place distributed practice in the top tier of study techniques.

why: Spacing retrieval out over time is one of the most robust findings in memory research, and one of the hardest to do consistently, because it needs the calendar as much as the lesson plan.
This routine solves the consistency problem by making the spacing automatic. Three questions per lesson, at three distances, and older material keeps reappearing without you having to track anything.
example: A geography teacher's starter slide carries the same three headings every lesson: yesterday, last week, last month. Writing tomorrow's slide is quick work with the medium term plan open. Pupils answer from memory before any books come out.
pages.try: Add the three headings to your existing starter template and fill them for one class tomorrow. The routine matters more than the perfect choice of questions.
notice: Which distance fails. If yesterday's question lands but last month's does not, that is the spacing doing its diagnostic work.
Whether the same older topic keeps failing. The card is explicit that the intervals are a starting point, and complex topics may need revisiting more often.
consider: It only works if the older material genuinely reappears, which makes this a planning habit as much as a lesson habit. The guide puts it well: the calendar is part of the pedagogy.
When content never returns after being taught, pupils conclude it no longer matters. This routine is the antidote, but only if you protect it when time is tight.
pages.wider: The spacing effect runs from Ebbinghaus through Cepeda's work on optimal gaps; Dunlosky's reviews rank distributed practice among the most effective techniques available.
tech: A low-stakes quiz tool, the approved one in your setting, takes the marking out of this entirely and keeps the routine sustainable; a spaced repetition tool can handle the intervals for you. What no tool should do is soften the retrieval itself. The struggle stays with the learner.

stair.lede: Drafting three questions at three distances, every lesson, is exactly the kind of repetitive drafting AI is good at, through the approved tool in your setting. A STAIR-shaped prompt does the heavy lifting:
stair.prompt:
Act as a secondary geography teacher. Create retrieval questions for a Year 8 class: one on yesterday's lesson (river landforms), one from last week (the water cycle), one from last month (map skills and grid references).

Keep every question answerable from memory in under a minute, focused on one precise idea, with no hints in the wording.

Keep the wording concise and do not include answers, explanations or extra detail.
stair.after: Swap in your own subject, class and topics, and expect to go back and forth before it's right. That's the I in STAIR: iteration is essential. You choose the questions; the tool just drafts them.

why: Blocked practice, finishing one topic before starting the next, feels organised, and pupils working through a block feel fluent. Kornell and Bjork found the feeling misleads: mixing topics produces stronger retention than blocking them.

The card names the mechanism: discriminating. When question types arrive shuffled, pupils must first decide what kind of problem they are looking at, and that decision is exactly what blocked practice never asks them to make.
example: A maths teacher setting practice on area swaps a page of fifteen area questions for a mixed set: area, perimeter and volume shuffled together. Pupils now have to choose the method before applying it. The work is slower and scrappier than the blocked version; the choosing is the added ingredient.
pages.try: Shuffle one existing practice set so that two or three related topics arrive mixed. Topics pupils can genuinely confuse give the discrimination something to bite on.
notice: Accuracy dipping during practice. Kornell and Bjork's point is that the dip in the lesson and the gain in retention tend to arrive together.
Whether pupils pause to classify a question before answering it. That pause is the mechanism working.
consider: Tell pupils why the practice feels harder. Without the explanation, interleaving reads as disorganisation, to them and sometimes to observers.
pages.wider: Kornell and Bjork's studies established the effect, and Rohrer's work in mathematics classrooms has tested it furthest from the laboratory.

why: The revision pattern the evidence ranks lowest, a single heavy session of re-reading close to the exam, is the one most pupils default to. Dunlosky's review placed re-reading among the least effective strategies; as the card says, many students do the opposite of what works.

This strategy is unusual in the guide because its audience is the pupils. Teach them the schedule itself: study, return after two days, then a week, then a month. It is knowledge about learning, taught like any other knowledge.
example: Ahead of mocks, a form tutor walks the class through building a revision timetable that returns to each subject at growing intervals rather than blocking one subject per evening. Pupils compare the plan with how they revised last time. Most find they had been doing the reverse.
pages.try: Next time you set revision, set the schedule as part of the task: which nights, returning to what, at which gaps. The gap sizes are a starting point, not a law.
notice: What pupils' current schedules actually look like. Ask before you teach the alternative; the contrast is the persuasive part.
Whether the schedule survives independently or collapses back into cramming. One walkthrough rarely changes habits on its own.
consider: Spacing feels less productive than cramming while you are doing it, which is partly why pupils abandon it. Teaching the schedule works better alongside teaching why it feels wrong.
pages.wider: Dunlosky and colleagues reviewed ten common study techniques and placed distributed practice near the top and re-reading near the bottom; this strategy hands that finding to the people doing the revising.

why: When a topic is taught, assessed and never seen again, pupils draw the sensible conclusion: it no longer matters. The card is blunt about this, and the fix is structural rather than heroic. Bring earlier content back in starters and assessments, planned at the level of the term, not improvised lesson by lesson.
Cumulative review is spacing applied to your planning documents. Nothing new gets taught; what changes is that older material keeps its place in the room.
example: A languages department agrees that every end-of-unit assessment will draw a quarter of its marks from earlier units. Vocabulary from September keeps appearing in January. Pupils stop treating each unit as disposable because, visibly, it is not.
pages.try: Look at your next planned assessment and add a small section drawn from a previous unit. Announce it in advance; the aim is to change what pupils keep revisiting, not to catch them out.
notice: How pupils respond when old content reappears. Surprise is evidence of the very expectation you are trying to change.
Which earlier topics have faded furthest; they are first in line for the next review slot.
consider: A question bank grows more useful every term you do this. Writing cumulative questions from scratch each time is the version of this strategy that does not survive a busy year.
pages.wider: Bjork's spacing research explains why the planned reappearances help; Carey, the card's other source, makes the same case for building return into the plan rather than leaving it to chance.

why: This is the idea underneath the whole retrieval guide, so it is worth meeting on its own terms. The conditions that make learning feel hard and slow in the moment, spacing it out, mixing it up, testing instead of reviewing, are often the very conditions that make it last. The conditions that feel smooth and productive mostly produce confidence without retention.

That runs against every instinct in a helpful profession. When a pupil struggles to retrieve, the natural move is to make it easier: a hint, a prompt, a quicker reveal. Bjork's work says the struggle is doing the useful work, provided what is being asked for was genuinely taught.
example: A teacher running a retrieval quiz turns the hints off and lengthens the silence before revealing answers. Pupils grumble that it feels harder than last term's version. Weeks later, the harder version is the one they remember.
pages.try: Take one retrieval activity you already run and remove one support: the hints, the word bank, or the notes-open first pass. Change nothing else, so you can see what the added difficulty does.
notice: The gap between how the activity feels and what it produces. Pupils rating it harder while recalling more, later, is the effect working as described.
Confident wrong answers. Difficulty exposes the illusion of knowing in a way smooth practice never does.
consider: Desirable difficulty is not the same as confusion. Difficulty from an unclear task or untaught content is just a barrier; the struggle has to be in the retrieving, not in working out what is being asked.
Secure the foundations first. Effortful retrieval works on knowledge that exists, which is why the guide pairs this idea with checking that the basics are in place before pushing beyond them.
How long to let the struggle run is not a rule anyone can hand you. That is a judgement made in the room, by the teacher who knows these students, watching whether the effort is still productive.
pages.wider: Bjork coined desirable difficulties for exactly this pattern, and the EEF's cognitive science review is a fair guide to how far the laboratory findings have travelled into classrooms.
tech: The card's tech line says it all: any retrieval tool, hints disabled. If the approved tool in your setting values speed, streaks or fastest-finger reveals, it's removing the desirable difficulty that makes the practice worthwhile. Retrieval is not a game show.

why: Retrieval with notes open is reading, not retrieval. The card's line is worth keeping whole, because it names the failure mode of plenty of well-intentioned practice: the format looks like a quiz while the support does the remembering.

The answer is not to ban support but to fade it on a schedule: notes first, then headings only, then nothing. The transition to unaided retrieval is where consolidation happens, so plan the fade as deliberately as you planned the support.
example: Reviewing a topic across three lessons, a teacher runs the same retrieval task each time with less on the table: full notes in the first, a five-heading skeleton in the second, a blank page in the third. Same questions, shrinking support.
pages.try: Take a retrieval activity your class currently does with notes open and run it next time with headings only. One step of the fade is enough to start.
notice: What happens at each step down. A sharp drop between notes and headings tells you the notes were doing the remembering.
Who freezes when the last support goes. Cued recall is the gentler step back for them.
consider: How fast to fade is a judgement made in the room; the teacher who knows the class can see whether the struggle is still productive, and no schedule on a website can.
Support removed too early produces confusion rather than desirable difficulty. The struggle has to be in the retrieving, not in guessing what is wanted.
tech: If you use an approved quiz tool for retrieval, its settings are part of the fade: hints off, closed-book or timed mode on, and any feature that supplies the answer at the first hesitation disabled. The tool should manage the activity, never the struggle.
pages.wider: Bjork's desirable difficulties frame the case for withdrawing support, and Kornell's work with him on how learners misread easy practice explains why the faded version feels worse than it is.

why: Knowledge practised in one format has a habit of staying there. Pupils who can answer the quiz version of a question can find the essay version unrecognisable, not because the knowledge is missing but because it is tied to the context it was learned in.

Godden and Baddeley showed decades ago that recall is bound to context. The card's response is to retrieve the same content in different formats and settings, decontextualising the knowledge on purpose. It is harder for students, and that is precisely the point.
example: One week a class retrieves the digestive system by labelling a diagram; the next, by writing a paragraph from memory; later, by answering spoken questions with no image in sight. The content stays fixed each time. What changes is everything around it.
pages.try: Take content the class has only ever retrieved one way and switch the format once: diagram to prose, written to spoken, multiple choice to free recall.
notice: The performance drop when the format changes. That gap is the context dependence you are trying to loosen, showing itself.
Whose knowledge already travels across formats and whose is bound to one. The second group had learned the format as much as the content.
consider: Vary the retrieval, not the goal. What is being retrieved stays the same; only its packaging moves.
pages.wider: Godden and Baddeley's diving study is the classic demonstration that recall is tied to the context it was encoded in; Bjork's work on varied practice turns that constraint into a teaching tactic.

why: Slamecka and Graf found that generating an answer, even a wrong one, before being told it produces stronger retention than passive exposure. Even a wrong one: the effort of generation drives the encoding, not the accuracy of the attempt.
This is the finding that licenses asking before telling. Whenever the answer arrives before pupils have attempted one, that effort never happens.
example: Introducing a new French verb, the teacher shows the infinitive and asks the class to guess the first-person form before revealing it. Half the guesses are wrong. Each pupil now has an attempt of their own to compare the answer against.
pages.try: Build one ask-before-tell moment into an explanation you already give: pose it, take guesses, then reveal. The guess costs seconds.
notice: Whether pupils will commit to a guess. A class trained to wait for the answer will need convincing that wrong attempts are welcome.
What the wrong guesses show about how pupils are thinking. They are a window as well as an encoding aid.
consider: The attempt must come before the answer, not instead of it. Generation works because the correction follows; leaving errors uncorrected is a different activity with different risks.
pages.wider: Slamecka and Graf named the generation effect in the 1970s; McDaniel's work has since carried it into more realistic educational materials.

why: The instinct after teaching something is to check it immediately, while it is fresh. Freshness is the problem. Quizzing straight after teaching mostly confirms what was said minutes ago, and the card is direct about the alternative: wait a day, then quiz. Wait a week, then quiz again.
A little forgetting first makes the retrieval effortful, and the effort is what strengthens the memory. The gap between learning and retrieval is where consolidation happens.
example: A teacher finishes explaining photosynthesis and, instead of quizzing on it in the plenary, quizzes on last week's respiration work. Photosynthesis gets its first quiz tomorrow and its second the following week.
pages.try: Move one end-of-lesson quiz to the start of the next lesson. Nothing else changes except the gap.
notice: Scores dropping compared with same-lesson quizzing. That drop is the point: the quiz is now measuring memory rather than echo.
Whether the week-later quiz shows the material coming back more securely than the day-later one did.
consider: Explain the delay to pupils. The gap is a design choice, and knowing that can make the harder quiz feel fair rather than punitive.
Checking understanding within the lesson still has its place; that is formative assessment doing a different job. What waits is the retrieval practice.
pages.wider: Bjork's work on spacing and Roediger's on the testing effect meet here: a test strengthens memory most when some forgetting has been allowed to happen first.

why: Retrieval is not a pub quiz. The card's warning is aimed at a real drift: retrieval routines that settle permanently at the level of dates, definitions and labelled diagrams, because those questions are the easiest to write and mark.

Agarwal's work behind this card cuts both ways. Factual retrieval builds the schema, so it is not beneath anyone; higher-order retrieval then tests whether students can use what the facts add up to. Secure the foundations first, then push beyond them.
example: After several factual quizzes on the causes of the Wall Street Crash, a history teacher's retrieval question changes shape: which cause mattered most, argued from memory in five sentences. The facts pupils have been retrieving for weeks become the material for a judgement.
pages.try: Audit a week of your retrieval questions against one test: could pupils answer these without understanding the topic? Add one question that requires using knowledge, not just producing it.
notice: Pupils fluent in factual rounds who stall at application. The knowledge may be present but unpractised in use.
What your question mix has drifted towards over a term. It is worth checking rather than assuming.
consider: Sequence matters. Higher-order retrieval on insecure foundations produces guessing, not thinking; the card's order, foundations first, is load-bearing.
pages.wider: Agarwal's studies of factual and higher-order quizzing sit directly behind this card, inside the testing effect tradition that runs from Roediger and Karpicke onwards.

why: The qualifier carries the strategy. Concept mapping with the notes open is an organising task; concept mapping from memory is retrieval, and Karpicke and Blunt found it outperformed re-reading for retention.
It also retrieves something a quiz rarely touches: the connections. Not just what students know but how the ideas relate. As the card has it, relational knowledge beats isolated facts.
example: Closing a unit on ecosystems, pupils get a blank page and one instruction: map the topic from memory, ideas in boxes, relationships written on the lines between them. Books stay shut. Afterwards they compare maps in pairs and add missing links in another colour.
pages.try: Run one from-memory map at the end of a current topic. Ask for the connecting lines to be labelled; an unlabelled line is a relationship nobody has had to retrieve.
notice: The links, more than the boxes. Missing ideas show gaps in knowledge; missing links show gaps in how it fits together.
Whether maps improve across the year. Mapping is itself a skill, and early attempts will understate what pupils know.
consider: The from-memory condition is the mechanism, so resist the merciful instinct to allow a peek at the notes. Checking comes afterwards, as its own step.
pages.wider: Karpicke and Blunt's study is the direct source, and it belongs to the broader testing effect tradition established by Roediger and Karpicke.

why: Anyone who has prepared to teach a topic knows the experience of discovering, mid-preparation, what they do not actually know. Preparing to teach demands complete, organised retrieval: gaps a quiz might skirt around become impossible to ignore when the whole thing has to be explained in order.
The card's emphasis is worth holding on to: the learning happens during preparation, not delivery. The audience is almost incidental. Organising knowledge to explain it is where consolidation occurs.
example: Pairs in a physics class each prepare a three-minute explanation of one circuit concept for another pair, from memory, with one diagram allowed. Most of the retrieval work is done before anyone speaks: deciding what comes first, what connects to what, and what they had to check.
pages.try: Set preparation-to-teach as the task without necessarily running the teaching. Planning an explanation of last month's topic is a complete retrieval activity on its own.
notice: What pupils look up while preparing. Each check against the notes is a self-identified gap.
The order pupils choose to explain things in. Sequencing choices show how their knowledge is organised.
consider: Delivery adds pressure that preparation does not, and whether a class is ready for peer teaching is the teacher's call, not the strategy's.
pages.wider: Nestojko and colleagues found that merely expecting to teach changes how people study; Fiorella and Mayer's work on learning by teaching locates the benefit in the organising and explaining itself.

why: Between showing pupils the answer and asking for it cold sits a wide, useful middle ground. Tulving and Thomson showed retrieval depends on the cues available; a heading, a keyword, a diagram with its labels removed each triggers retrieval without doing the work.
Treat it as a rung, not a destination. Cued recall builds confidence before unaided retrieval, and it is a gentler restart for pupils who freeze at a blank page.
example: A pupil who produced almost nothing in a free brain dump gets the same task with the topic's five subheadings printed down the margin. The headings cue what order things come in; the remembering between them is still the pupil's.
pages.try: Keep a cued version of your usual retrieval task ready: the same questions with a keyword or first letter alongside. Moving one pupil down to it costs nothing.
notice: Which cues bring the memory back and which draw blank looks. A cue that does nothing suggests the memory it points at was never secure in the first place.
Who still needs the cues after several rounds. The aim is to retire them, pupil by pupil.
consider: Cues can drift into being answers. A sentence starter that contains the key term has crossed the line from triggering retrieval to replacing it.
Pair this with a plan to fade. Cued recall that never becomes unaided recall stops short of where consolidation happens.

stair.lede: Turning your notes into gapped versions is repetitive drafting, which makes it a fair job for AI through the approved tool in your setting:
stair.prompt:
Act as a secondary history teacher. Take the key points below about the causes of the First World War and create a gapped version for Year 9 cued recall, removing one key term per sentence and listing the removed words separately.

Keep every sentence otherwise word for word as supplied. Do not add new content, explanations or answers beside the gaps.

[paste your key points here]
stair.after: Because the tool only removes words from text you supply, what pupils retrieve is still exactly what you taught. Check the gaps target the terms that carry the meaning, and iterate if they don't.

pages.wider: Tulving and Thomson's encoding specificity work established that what can be recalled depends on the cues present at retrieval; this strategy puts that finding to deliberate use.
tech: A cloze quiz or gapped handout tool, approved in your setting, builds the cued step quickly and lets you fade the cues over successive attempts.

why: Pupils' judgements of what they know are systematically off, and mostly off in one direction. Familiar material feels known; Koriat and Bjork traced how that feeling misleads. The result is revision effort spent in the wrong places, with complete sincerity.

You cannot lecture the illusion away. The card's move is to let pupils catch themselves in it: rate confidence before the answer is revealed, then look at where certainty and correctness came apart. When they were certain and wrong, that is the precise moment to intervene.
example: Before each answer in a quiz review is revealed, pupils hold up one to five fingers for confidence. On question four, half the class shows five fingers and the revealed answer proves most of them wrong. The teacher stops the quiz there. That question, not the quiz score, becomes the discussion.
pages.try: Add a confidence rating to one quiz you already run: sure, unsure, guessing is enough of a scale. The comparison with the revealed answers does the teaching.
notice: Where high confidence meets wrong answers. Those items are the strategy's whole target.
Whether calibration improves over the weeks: fewer certain-and-wrong moments is what progress looks like here.
consider: Confident errors want fast correction; Metcalfe's finding on instant feedback applies most exactly here.
Keep the ratings private at first if being wrong in public carries a social cost in this class. The teacher knows whether a class can be wrong out loud; a website does not.
pages.wider: Koriat and Bjork documented the illusion of knowing, and Dunlosky's metacognition research shows how loosely felt confidence tracks actual retention.

why: This card holds two instructions in tension on purpose. Metcalfe shows instant feedback is essential for confident errors: the more certain a pupil was, the more the fast correction helps. For general retrieval, though, a processing gap before revealing answers gives the retrieval attempt room to finish.
So the rule the card offers is about targeting: speed matters most when confidence is highest.
example: Running a review quiz, a teacher reveals each answer a beat or two after the question rather than instantly, letting pupils commit. When a show of hands exposes a confidently wrong majority on one item, the delay disappears: that misconception gets corrected on the spot.
pages.try: Next quiz, delay each reveal until every pupil has committed an answer, and break your own rule the moment you spot a confident error.
notice: What pupils do in the gap before the reveal. Reconsidering and committing means the gap is being used; passive waiting suggests it is just dead air.
Whether corrected confident errors stay corrected the following week. Metcalfe's work suggests they often may.
consider: Instant feedback and instant answers are different things. Feedback follows an attempt; a tool that supplies the answer at the first pause has replaced the attempt.
tech: Quiz tools with instant answer reveal are built for exactly half of this card. The reveal speed is usually a setting, so check whether the approved tool in your setting can hold answers back until responses are in. And if the format starts to resemble a fastest finger first round, rewarding speed over thought, it is stripping out the difficulty that makes the retrieval worth doing.
pages.wider: Metcalfe's research on error correction, including the finding that high-confidence errors are especially correctable, is the direct source for the card's distinction.

why: Students are most confident about the things they read most recently, not the things they actually know. That is Dunlosky and Metcalfe's finding, and it explains a great deal of misdirected revision: recency masquerades as mastery, and decisions get made on the feeling.
Rating confidence after each retrieval attempt, then revealing the answer, turns that private feeling into something that can be checked. The gap between the rating and the result is the target.
example: In a self-quizzing routine, pupils answer each question, write 1 to 5 for how sure they are, then check. One pupil finds her 5s are mostly right, but so are her 2s: she knows more than she feels she does, and her revision list changes accordingly.
pages.try: Add a one-number confidence column to any answer-then-check activity the class already does. The overhead is seconds per question.
notice: Systematic patterns: pupils always certain, pupils never certain. Both are calibration problems, and they need different conversations.
Whether the ratings change what pupils choose to revise. The number is only worth collecting if it changes a decision.
consider: Rate after the attempt, not before it. The card is specific, because the attempt itself is evidence the rating should draw on.
pages.wider: Dunlosky and Metcalfe's work on metacognitive monitoring is the direct source: judgements of learning track recency and fluency more faithfully than they track actual knowledge.

why: Most retrieval activity evaporates the moment it ends. The quiz happened, some things came back and some did not, and by next week nobody, pupil included, remembers which was which.

A retrieval journal keeps the record: what came back, what did not, what needs revisiting. Zimmerman showed students who monitor their performance make better revision decisions, and the card frames the journal accordingly: it is a map of what to do next, not a diary.
example: After each Friday quiz, pupils spend three minutes on a two-column log: came back, did not. The did-not column from the last month becomes their personal starter list for revision week. No teacher marking is involved at any point.
pages.try: Two columns in the back of the exercise book is a complete version of this. Start after your next retrieval activity.
notice: Whether the journal changes behaviour. A log nobody consults is admin; the test is what pupils choose to revisit.
Recurring entries in the did-not column. Content a pupil logs as missing three times is a message addressed to you as much as to them.
consider: Keep the logging light. Three minutes of honest record beats ten minutes of decorated reflection, and marking it changes what pupils are willing to record.
pages.wider: Zimmerman's self-regulation research supplies the case for monitoring; Dunlosky's reviews supply the strategies the journal should steer pupils towards.

why: Dunlosky's review rated ten common study strategies: re-reading scored low and practice testing scored highest. Most pupils have never seen that table, and their revision habits show it.
The strategy is a structured comparison: ask students how they revise, then show them the evidence. As the card puts it, that conversation is the intervention.
example: Before study leave, a tutor group lists their revision methods anonymously on slips. The tally goes on the board next to a summary of Dunlosky's ratings. Re-reading and highlighting dominate the class list and sit near the bottom of the evidence table; the session is spent on the gap between the two columns.
notice: The reasons pupils give for their current habits. It feels productive and I have always done it this way are exactly what the desirable difficulties research predicts, and worth naming aloud.
Whether anything shifts by the next audit. Run it twice a year; the second tally is your evidence of movement.
consider: The point is not to shame current habits but to replace them. Pair the audit with teaching an alternative, such as the retrieval schedule, so the conversation ends with something to do.
pages.wider: Dunlosky and colleagues' review of ten study techniques is the whole evidence base here; the audit simply puts its findings in front of the people they are about.

why: A class can finish every task you set and still miss the learning the tasks were built to serve. The intention is what to learn; the task is the vehicle. When the two blur, pupils judge success by completion, and in the rush of a lesson, so can the teacher.
Keeping them distinct changes small, practical things: how you introduce the work, what you praise while pupils are doing it, and what you actually check at the end.
example: In history, the task is a paragraph on the causes of the First World War; the intention is to understand how long term tensions and short term triggers interact. The teacher frames the paragraph as one way of showing that understanding, and the end-of-lesson check asks about the interaction, not whether the paragraph got finished.
pages.try: In your next plan, write the intention and the task on separate lines. If you cannot state the intention without describing the task, that is worth a second look before the lesson.
notice: What pupils say when asked what they are learning. 'A poster' is a task answer; the idea behind the poster is the learning answer.
Whether your own checks at the end of the lesson assess the learning or the completion.
consider: The card asks for the separation at every stage, in planning and in what you say to pupils. It is easiest to hold at the start of a lesson and easiest to lose in the middle of a busy one.
pages.wider: Clarifying learning intentions is the first of Wiliam's formative assessment strands: the answer to where the learner is going has to be about the learning, not the activity.

why: Criteria handed to a class arrive as your words, and your words carry your understanding, not theirs. Asking pupils what excellent looks like before they begin makes them do the analysis themselves, and the card is plain about why: criteria they articulate themselves land far more deeply than criteria handed to them.
The discussion is also evidence in its own right. What a class can and cannot name about quality tells you what they can and cannot yet see in good work.
example: Before a piece of persuasive writing, the class reads a strong letter and lists what makes it work. The teacher collects suggestions, tidies overlaps, and the list on the board, in the pupils' own phrasing, becomes the checklist they draft against.
pages.try: Next time you would normally display a success criteria slide, hold it back. Ask the class first, and see how much of your slide they build without you.
notice: The gap between what pupils propose and what you would have written. Missing criteria show you what they cannot yet recognise in good work.
Whether pupils refer back to the list while working, or whether it stays on the board as decoration.
consider: Their language becoming the standard does not mean any list will do. You still steer: collecting, sharpening, and adding what the class cannot yet name, so the final criteria are both theirs and right.
This pairs naturally with exemplars. Criteria are far easier for pupils to generate from work they can see than from a blank instruction.
pages.wider: Wiliam and Leahy include co-constructed criteria among their practical techniques for clarifying and sharing what quality means, so that the standard is understood rather than merely displayed.

why: Rubrics describe quality; exemplars demonstrate it. A pupil can read 'uses precise vocabulary' and nod along without any idea what precision looks like in this subject at this level. Put two pieces of work side by side and the difference becomes something they can point at.
There is a second advantage the card names: pupils spot quality in someone else's work more readily than in their own. Judging an exemplar is rehearsal for judging themselves.
example: Before a design evaluation, a technology teacher puts two anonymised evaluations from a previous year under the visualiser, one strong, one mid-standard. Pupils identify the differences in pairs, and those differences become the criteria for their own writing.
pages.try: Save two or three anonymised pieces from this year's classes. That is the whole preparation; next year's lesson starts with them.
notice: The features pupils identify unprompted, and the ones they miss entirely. What they miss is what still needs teaching.
Whether the qualities they named in the exemplar show up in their own work afterwards.
consider: The card says work at different standards, not just a single model of excellence. The contrast between pieces is where the noticing happens.
Use work from other classes or previous years where you can. Whether a current pupil's work can be shown, even anonymised, is a judgement for the teacher who knows the class.
pages.wider: Sadler argued that pupils can only close a gap in quality they can actually perceive; Berger's work on models of excellence makes the same case from the classroom, with standards caught from real work rather than descriptions of it.

why: Copying an objective from the board at the start of a lesson produces writing, not thinking. Asking pupils to name what they learned at the end demands both: they have to survey the lesson and generate the answer themselves.
It also hands you a small piece of evidence you cannot get any other way: whether what they think the lesson was about matches what you think you taught. The two are not always the same.
example: At the end of a science lesson, pupils write one sentence: what was today actually about? The teacher reads a handful aloud. Half the class describe the activity rather than the idea behind it, which tells the teacher exactly what to sharpen next lesson.
pages.try: Once this week, skip the copied objective and ask for the sentence at the end instead. Compare what they write with what you had planned on the board.
notice: Answers that describe the task rather than the learning. The guide draws that line deliberately: finishing the task is not the same as achieving the learning.
How close the class's version is to yours. A wide gap is not a failed lesson; it is unusually honest feedback on the teaching.
consider: Withholding the objective is not the same as hiding the point. Pupils still need clarity about what they are doing and why while they work; what changes is who articulates the learning, and when.

Some schools expect objectives visible in every lesson. How this routine sits with that expectation is a judgement for the teacher in the room. You know your class and your context better than any guide does.
pages.wider: The mechanism is the generation effect: Slamecka and Graf found that producing an answer embeds it more reliably than copying one, even when the produced answer needs correcting.

why: Every lesson has a turning point where you decide, usually on a feeling, whether the class is ready to move on. A hinge question replaces the feeling with evidence: one diagnostic question, placed at the hinge, answered by everyone.

What makes it a hinge question rather than just a question is the design of the wrong answers. Each one maps to a misconception you already know pupils hold, so the spread of responses tells you not just how many are stuck but why.
example: A maths teacher planning a lesson on adding fractions writes one question for the midpoint, with four responses: the right answer, the classic add-tops-and-bottoms error, a common denominator slip, and a simplification mistake. Every pupil answers at once on whiteboards. The room's spread decides the second half of the lesson.
pages.try: Plan a single hinge question for one lesson next week. Write the wrong answers first, from the errors you already see in books, then build the question around them.
notice: Which distractor gets chosen. That is the diagnosis, and it is more useful than the count of correct answers.
What you actually did next. As the guide has it, evidence has done nothing until it changes what happens in the following five minutes.
consider: The card's warning deserves its own line: never improvise it. An improvised hinge question collapses into a recall check with no diagnostic power.
It needs an all-pupil response method to work; a hinge answered by three volunteers is a hinge in name only.
One good hinge per lesson is plenty. The cost is planning time, which is exactly why the wrong answers are worth engineering carefully once and reusing.
pages.wider: This comes from Dylan Wiliam's formative assessment work: assessment moved out of the marking pile and into the lesson, where it can still change the teaching.
tech: A polling or quiz tool, the approved one in your setting, gets you the whole room's answer at the hinge in seconds, with the spread visible instantly. The tool has done nothing until what it shows changes your next five minutes.

stair.lede: The expensive part of a hinge question is drafting distractors that map to real misconceptions. AI, through the approved tool in your setting, can draft them for you to judge. A STAIR-shaped prompt looks like this:
stair.prompt:
Act as a primary teacher who is a science specialist and create hinge questions on the water cycle for Year 5. Keep tightly to evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection.

Present the output in clearly labelled sections and ensure each hinge question is quick to answer, focused on one precise idea and suitable as a decision point in the lesson. Ensure questions elicit the ability for Year 5 to apply their understanding with confidence.

Every hinge question must include plausible distractors based on age-appropriate misconceptions so teachers can interpret pupils' thinking accurately. Keep the wording concise and avoid unnecessary detail, explanations or answers.
stair.after: Swap the role, topic and year group for your own. Then do the part only you can do: check each distractor against the misconceptions your pupils actually hold, and iterate until they match. That's the I in STAIR, and it's where the diagnostic power comes from.

why: A multiple choice question with throwaway wrong answers tells you one thing: right or wrong. Engineer each distractor to map onto a real misconception and the same question tells you why a pupil is wrong, which is the information you can actually teach from. As the card has it, wrong answers are the diagnostic data.
example: For a question on photosynthesis, a science teacher writes three distractors from errors seen in books: plants get their food from the soil, plants only respire at night, and oxygen is what plants take in rather than give out. Whichever option a pupil picks, the teacher knows which idea to revisit.
pages.try: Take one question you already use and rewrite its wrong answers from the errors in your current marking. The misconceptions are already in the books; the work is moving them into the options.
notice: Which distractor draws the most pupils. The pattern is more useful than the score.
A distractor nobody ever picks. It tells you nothing; replace it with an error pupils actually make.
Whether the same misconception resurfaces weeks later. A question worth engineering once is worth reusing.
consider: This is where the planning cost of a hinge question lives, and why the card treats the wrong answers as carefully as the right one. Improvised distractors collapse the diagnosis.
tech: The approved quiz tool in your setting that shows the full spread of responses, not just the proportion correct, is what turns carefully built distractors into evidence: you can see at a glance which misconception the room holds, from every pupil at once rather than the few who would have spoken. The chart has done nothing, though, until it changes what you teach in the next five minutes.
pages.wider: Diagnostic questioning built on known misconceptions runs through Black and Wiliam's account of eliciting evidence: the point of asking is to find out what pupils actually think, not to confirm what you hope they think.

why: Hands up samples the confident. Random selection is fairer, but it is still chance, and chance can leave the same pupils unheard for weeks. Choosing who answers on purpose lets you reach the thinking you most need to hear: the pupil whose book worried you, the one who has not spoken since Tuesday.
Tracking participation is what makes the deliberateness honest. Memory flatters; a record shows you who has actually stayed invisible across lessons.
example: A teacher keeps a simple tally of who has answered across the week. Before Friday's lesson she reads it back, finds three pupils with no entries, and plans a question for each, matched to material they have had time to think about.
pages.try: For one class, track who answers for a week, by whatever means is least effort. Read the record before planning the next lesson and let it choose two of your questions.
notice: Who the record says you have not heard from. It is rarely who you would have guessed.
How responses change once the class knows anyone might be asked, not just the raised hands.
consider: 'Where appropriate' is doing real work in the card. Which pupils to press, and when a quieter route to a pupil's thinking serves better than a public question, is a call for the teacher who knows the class, not a website.
tech: An approved participation tracking tool in your setting can carry the record for you, and its contribution is memory, not judgement. It shows who has stayed invisible across lessons; deciding who to call, and why, stays with you.
pages.wider: Hearing from all learners rather than a self-selecting few is central to Wiliam and Black's case for assessment that happens during the lesson, while it can still change the teaching.

why: The classic weakness of classroom questioning is that you hear from a handful of pupils and make assumptions about the rest. Mini whiteboards remove the assumption: every pupil answers, every answer is visible, and you read the whole room in seconds.
They also change who participates. There is no waiting for a turn and no hiding behind the confident few, which is why this one strategy appears in so many of the routes through this site.
example: A languages teacher checking verb endings asks the class to write the conjugation and hold boards up together on a count of three. Thirty answers appear at once. Two errors dominate, so the next five minutes deal with those two errors rather than moving on.
pages.try: One all-write, all-show question at tomorrow's key checkpoint. Showing together matters; staggered reveals let pupils copy the early boards.
notice: The answers from pupils you would never have called on. That is the evidence you have been missing.
How quickly you can read the room, and what you do when the room disagrees with your plan.
consider: Boards suit short-form answers. For extended reasoning you will need a different route to the same visibility.
The point is the evidence, not the equipment. If the routine drifts into a game of speed, the quality of the answers, and the diagnosis, goes with it.
pages.wider: Eliciting evidence from every pupil is one of Wiliam and Black's core formative assessment moves; the whiteboard is simply the cheapest reliable way to do it.
tech: Multimodal response tools, through the approved tool in your setting, do the same job when you need typed answers, anonymity or a record: every learner visible at once. The test is identical either way: a screen full of responses has done nothing until it changes what you do next.

why: Four cards per pupil, one question, every answer in the air at once. The routine costs almost nothing, and what it buys is the thing this strand keeps returning to: a response from everyone, not a guess about the room built from three raised hands.
No hands, no opt-out also changes what answering feels like. Nobody is volunteering; everyone is simply answering, which lowers the cost of being wrong in front of others.
example: A geography teacher poses a four-option question on reading a population pyramid. On a count of three, thirty cards go up. A visible cluster on option C, the misread axis, decides what gets explained next.
pages.try: A class set costs one preparation session: print, laminate if you like, keep them in the room. Start with a single question at one checkpoint tomorrow.
notice: The spread, not just the most common answer. A room split two ways needs different teaching from a room that is mostly right.
Pupils who glance sideways before raising their card. Simultaneity is what protects the evidence.
consider: The question has to deserve the routine. Four options invite properly engineered distractors; a question with three filler answers wastes the whole-class machinery.
Cards suit selected response. When you need to see working or prose, mini whiteboards or another route to the same full visibility does that job.
pages.wider: All-student response is one of Wiliam's staple techniques for eliciting evidence: the next teaching decision gets made on the whole room, not a sample of it.

why: Whatever method you use to gather responses decides, before any pupil starts answering, who gets to show what they know. Oral questioning favours the quick and the confident; written answers favour fluent writers; a single fixed method excludes the same pupils every time.

Offering written, verbal, visual and digital routes is not variety for its own sake. It is about the evidence: a pupil who cannot respond through the channel you chose reads as not knowing, when the truth may be that they could not show it.
example: Checking understanding of a novel's turning point, a teacher accepts a sentence, a labelled sketch of the scene, or a short spoken answer on a class device. Two pupils who rarely write anything hand in sketches the teacher can read as evidence like any written answer.
pages.try: Pick one routine check you already run and offer a second way to answer it. One alternative channel is enough to see who it reaches.
notice: Which pupils change when the channel changes. That difference is information about the method, not the pupil.
Whether anonymity shifts the honesty of what comes back, especially on questions about confusion.
consider: More channels means more to read. Choose the checkpoints where the evidence justifies it rather than multiplying options in every task.
Which pupils need which route, and when a pupil should be stretched beyond a comfortable channel, is the teacher's call. The card sets the principle, not the prescription.
tech: Multimodal and anonymous response tools, the approved ones in your setting, are where this principle most obviously meets technology: they can gather a response from every learner at once, in more than one form, and anonymity can make honest answers easier to give. The test stays the same as for every tool in this strand: the responses only count as formative once they change what you do next.
pages.wider: The principle comes from CAST's Universal Design for Learning framework: multiple means of action and expression, so that the method of responding does not decide who appears to understand.

why: Think, pair, share fails in predictable ways: no individual thinking before the talking starts, pairs where one voice does all the work, and a share stage answered by whoever volunteers. The disciplined version closes each gap in turn.

Nomination carries the most weight. When any pupil might report back, the pair talk has to leave both partners able to answer, and the share becomes evidence about the room rather than a performance by the most confident voice.
example: In RE, pupils get one silent minute to note their own answer, two timed minutes to compare in pairs, and then the teacher names who reports back. Because nobody knew who would be chosen, both partners in each pair had a reason to make sure both could answer.
pages.try: Add the timer and the nomination to a think, pair, share you already use. Tell the class before the talk begins that you will choose who shares; that single sentence is the discipline.
notice: Whether the silent minute is actually silent. The individual think is the stage most often skipped, and the one the paired talk depends on.
What nominated pupils report: their own view, their partner's, or a genuine combination of the two.
consider: A visible timer for the pair stage holds the structure without you policing it.
Nominating kindly is a skill in itself. How much warning a particular pupil needs before speaking to the room is a judgement for the teacher who knows them.
pages.wider: Wiliam's treatment of classroom talk keeps returning to the same move: structures that make evidence of thinking part of the routine rather than something volunteered.

why: Butler's finding is stark enough that the card leads with it: comments alone produced the greatest gains, and adding a grade to the comment cancelled it out. Given both, pupils read the grade, compare it with their neighbour's, and the comment might as well not be there.
Removing grades from work in progress protects the only part of the marking that can still change the work.
example: A maths teacher returns a practice paper with comments identifying the strongest section and the step where marks were lost, and no score anywhere. The first ten minutes of the lesson go on acting on those comments; scores appear only when the unit's final assessment arrives.
pages.try: Choose one piece of work in progress from one class and mark it comment only. Watch what pupils do with the comments when there is no grade to look at first.
notice: Where pupils' eyes go when work comes back, and how many read past a grade when one is present.
Whether your comments give pupils something to do rather than something to feel.
consider: Work in progress is the card's boundary. Summative pieces still get graded; the change protects feedback while the work can still improve.

Some marking policies expect grades on every piece. How comment only marking sits with that expectation is a judgement for the teacher in the room, and sometimes a conversation in the department, not a rule a website can settle.
pages.wider: Butler compared grades, comments and the two combined; the gains sat with comments alone, and the combination did no better than grades by themselves.

why: The card sets a simple test: feedback must be more work for the recipient than the donor. Most written marking fails it. A corrected error requires nothing of the pupil except to read it, or not; a question about the error requires an answer.
The card's other line is worth keeping whole: if feedback requires no response from the learner, it is not feedback; it is merely information.
example: Instead of correcting a misused apostrophe, a teacher writes: there are two apostrophe errors in this paragraph; find and fix both. The pupil does the locating and the correcting, which is where the thinking sits.
pages.try: In your next round of marking, convert your five most common corrections into five reusable questions. The stock builds quickly and cuts the writing time.
notice: Whether pupils actually respond, and in what depth. A question ignored has caused no more thinking than a correction.
The ratio of your effort to theirs, page by page. The card's test is blunt, which makes it easy to apply.
consider: Time for the response has to exist somewhere in a lesson. A question with no time set aside to answer it is a correction with extra steps.
tech: An approved annotation tool with a reply function in your setting makes the response visible: every question you leave either has an answer against it or does not, for every pupil, and that record can shape what the next lesson revisits. The questions still have to be worth answering; the tool only shows you whether they were.
pages.wider: This is Wiliam's framing of feedback inside formative assessment: the purpose is to cause thinking that closes the gap, not to document errors.

why: Feedback given at the end of a unit, with nothing left to apply it to, is a record rather than an intervention. The card's fix is structural: the next lesson begins with pupils reading and responding to their feedback before anything new arrives.
Those first minutes are what make the marking you have already done worth the hours it took.
example: Books go back at the start of the lesson. Pupils spend the opening ten minutes on their responses: answering the questions left in the margins, redrafting one sentence, correcting a method. New content waits until the responses are done.
pages.try: Protect the first ten minutes of one lesson this week for acting on feedback. Nothing else changes; the feedback you were going to give anyway now has somewhere to land.
notice: What pupils do unprompted with the time, which tells you how actionable the feedback actually was.
Whether responses engage with the gap you identified. A tick and 'done' next to an unchanged answer is a response in name only.
consider: Sharing feedback in advance, where your school's systems allow it, means the lesson time starts at the responding rather than the reading.
If there is never time to act on it, the honest question is whether the feedback needed writing at all. The card puts it more bluntly: feedback with no time to act on it has no value.
pages.wider: Wiliam and Leahy treat time to act as part of the feedback itself rather than an optional follow-up: feedback moves learning forward only while the work can still change.

why: Thirty individual comments take hours and reach one pupil each. Reading the set for patterns takes a fraction of the time and produces something you can teach with: the class's common strengths, its recurring errors, and two or three next steps for everyone.
Teach to the gap, not to the individual paper, as the card has it. The gaps repeat far more often than the papers do.
example: After reading a set of essays without writing on them, a teacher notes on a single page: conclusions strong across the class, evidence rarely linked back to the question, three recurring misconceptions. The next lesson teaches the linking move to everyone, then pupils revisit their own essays looking for it.
pages.try: Next marking session, read the whole set before writing anything. One page of patterns, then decide what the following lesson does about them.
notice: Whether the recurring errors actually recur less after being taught to. That is the test of the next steps you chose.
Pupils who do not fit the patterns, in either direction. Whole class feedback still needs eyes on the outliers.
consider: The saving is in the writing, not the attention. Patterns are only as good as the reading that finds them.
The card offers this as a way of keeping workload manageable, not a rule that no pupil ever gets an individual comment. Where individual response is still needed is your call.
pages.wider: It draws on Wiliam's case for evidence that changes the teaching, and on Hattie's finding that feedback helps most when it is specific about the next step in the work rather than about the person.

why: A correction does the cognitive work for the pupil and hopes some of it rubs off. A question hands the work back. Returning a piece with three questions rather than a page of corrections keeps the effort where the card says it belongs: with the learner.
Three is a discipline as much as a number. Choosing which three to ask forces you to decide which gaps deserve the pupil's limited attention.
example: On a science investigation write-up, instead of correcting the method section, the teacher writes: which variable did you actually change? How would a reader repeat step 3? What would make your conclusion safer? The pupil answers all three before starting the next investigation.
pages.try: Trial it on one set of books: three questions, no corrections, and the requirement that answers come before new work. The requirement is the part that cannot be skipped.
notice: The quality of the answers. Thin ones usually mean the question told the pupil what to write.
How long the questions take to write compared with your usual marking of the same work.
consider: The 'must respond before moving on' clause carries the whole strategy. Questions without protected time to answer them collapse back into corrections that happen to have question marks.
pages.wider: The reasoning is Wiliam's: feedback should cause thinking, and correcting on the pupil's behalf removes the struggle the learning depends on.

why: Between your model and independent work there is a gap, and pupils fall into it at predictable points. Structured practice with peers, checked at every stage, puts a floor under that gap: nobody moves to step four carrying an unnoticed error from step two.
The card's first line sets the frame: independence is the destination, not the starting point.
example: Learning to balance chemical equations, pairs work through four equations one at a time, comparing answers after each and resolving disagreements before the next. The teacher circulates listening for pairs who agree on a wrong answer, since those are the errors that will not surface on their own.
pages.try: Take a practice set you already use and add one rule: check with your partner after every item, not at the end. The per-stage check is the difference between guided practice and marking each other's finished work.
notice: Pairs who agree quickly on wrong answers. Peer checking catches disagreement; confident shared errors need you.
The point where the checking starts to slow pupils who are ready to work alone. That is the signal to remove the structure, not tighten it.
consider: The staging does the work here. A check at the end of a whole exercise arrives after the errors have compounded; a check at every stage is what stops them compounding at all.
pages.wider: Guided practice with a high success rate before independent work is one of Rosenshine's principles of instruction, drawn from studies of what the most effective teachers actually do.

why: Answering a question exercises what a pupil knows. Writing one that could plausibly appear in an assessment demands more: surveying the topic, judging which ideas are assessable, and knowing the material well enough to say what a fair question and a correct answer look like. The card puts it directly: generating questions demands higher order thinking than simply answering them.
The questions also come back to you as evidence. What pupils choose to ask, and what they avoid, maps the topic as they see it.
example: Closing a unit on rivers, each pupil writes two possible assessment questions with answers. The teacher collates the strongest into next week's review quiz, and notices that almost nobody has written a question about deposition, which says something about where the class's confidence runs out.
pages.try: End one topic with: write two questions that could be on the test, with answers. Use the best of them in your next review.
notice: The level of the questions: pure recall, or questions that need explanation and application to answer.
The topics nobody writes questions about. Avoidance is data too.
consider: A vague or unanswerable question usually points at a gap in understanding the content, not the task, which makes it worth following up rather than discarding.
pages.wider: Black and Wiliam place this kind of activity with students as resources for, and owners of, their own learning: the assessment thinking starts to move from teacher to pupil.

why: Peer assessment has a bad name in classrooms where it means swapping books and hunting for spelling errors. The card locates the fault precisely: without shared criteria, peer feedback is opinion, not evidence.

The structure starts before any assessing happens. Pupils who have examined exemplars and agreed what quality looks like have a standard to assess against; pupils who have not can only compare the work with their own taste.
example: Before assessing each other's speeches, the class watches two recorded examples and agrees what separated them. Only then do pairs assess, against that agreed list, with one rule: every judgement has to point to a specific moment in the speech.
pages.try: Before your next peer assessment, insert one exemplar discussion and have the class agree the criteria they will use. Same task, one added step.
notice: Whether feedback cites the shared criteria or drifts back to personal preference.
How pupils receive peer judgements compared with yours, and whether criteria they helped build change that.
consider: Pairings carry social weight. Who assesses whom, and whether some work is better assessed anonymously, is exactly the kind of call the teacher in the room makes and a website cannot.
pages.wider: Sadler's argument is that any assessor needs a concept of quality they can apply; Berger's classroom practice shows pupils building that concept from real examples of excellent work.

why: Quizzing on today's lesson checks whether the teaching landed. Quizzing on last month's checks something this strand cares about more: whether the learning survived. Returning to older material at increasing intervals is, as the card notes, one of the most robust findings in memory research.
It sits in a formative assessment strand because the results are evidence. What the class has forgotten tells you what needs revisiting before it is needed again.
example: A weekly low stakes quiz in history draws two questions from last week, two from the last unit, and one from the autumn term. The autumn question is the one most pupils miss, so it returns in a different form the following week.
pages.try: Add one deliberately old question to a quiz routine you already run. One question is enough to start seeing what has faded.
notice: The gap between performance on recent and older material. That gap is the forgetting the spacing works against.
Whether pupils treat wrong answers as information or as failure. The low stakes framing has to be real, not just announced.
consider: Increasing intervals is the principle; re-reading is the trap. The card is explicit that re-reading notes is not the same as retrieving, and pupils will default to it because it feels easier.

How far apart the returns come is a professional judgement for the teacher in the room, made with this class and this content in front of them. Increasing intervals is the fixed principle; the calendar that delivers it is yours.
pages.wider: The tradition here is Bjork's work on desirable difficulties: spacing and retrieval both make practice feel harder now in exchange for retention later.

why: Putting a question to a class questions they cannot yet be expected to answer looks pointless. The card's mechanism says otherwise: triggering the feeling of not knowing primes attention for the explanation that follows, and pupils who struggle towards an answer before instruction remember the real one better.
There is a second yield for the teacher: the pre-quiz shows you what the class already knows, and which misconceptions are arriving with them, before you decide where the teaching needs its weight.
example: Before a unit on electricity, a short ungraded quiz asks pupils to predict what happens to bulbs in series and parallel circuits. The wrong predictions surface the familiar current-gets-used-up idea, and the first lesson is built to confront it.
pages.try: Open your next new topic with five questions pupils cannot yet be expected to answer, framed exactly that way: you are not supposed to know this yet; have a go anyway.
notice: How the same questions land after the teaching. The before-and-after pair is the clearest picture of what the unit added.
Whether the framing holds. If pupils experience the pre-quiz as a test, the low stakes are gone and so is the willingness to guess.
consider: The mechanism runs on struggle, so failing at the start has to be explicitly safe. That is set by how you introduce it and how you react to the wrong answers, not by the quiz itself.
pages.wider: Pre-testing belongs to Bjork's family of desirable difficulties; Wiliam's interest is in the same activity read as evidence of where learners are before the teaching starts.

why: Asking a class whether they understand invites the least reliable answer in teaching. Asking each pupil, anonymously, what they are least clear about gets you the truth, because nobody has to own a confusion publicly.
Two minutes at the end of a lesson buys you the agenda for the start of the next one, drawn from the pupils' actual sticking points rather than your guess at them.
example: Last two minutes: every pupil writes the one thing from today they are least sure about, no names, slips in a box on the way out. Three pupils name the same step in the method. The next lesson opens by reteaching that step to everyone.
pages.try: Run it tomorrow with slips of paper or an anonymous form, whichever is less fuss. The only rule that matters is that the most common muddy point gets addressed, publicly, next lesson.
