notice: Clusters. One pupil's confusion is individual; eight naming the same idea is a teaching point.
The pupils who write nothing is muddy, every time. Certainty that consistent deserves a quiet check of its own.
consider: The loop has to close. If muddy points vanish into the box and never resurface, pupils stop telling you the truth within a fortnight.
Keep it anonymous. The honesty is the entire value, and it evaporates the moment names go on slips.
pages.wider: The technique comes out of the classroom assessment tradition in higher education, and it survives in schools for the same reason: honest evidence at almost no cost.
tech: An anonymous response tool in your setting's approved list makes the collection frictionless and genuinely nameless, which protects the honesty this depends on. Slips of paper in a box do the same job; choose whichever your pupils will trust.

why: Rosenshine begins his principles with review for a reason: in the classroom studies, the most effective teachers opened lessons with it and checked understanding constantly. A brief review of prior content, every lesson, keeps older learning warm and gives you a running read on what has stuck.
The card carries its own decision rule: if most pupils cannot answer, adjust the pace of teaching. The review is evidence collection with a consequence attached, not a settling activity.
example: Five questions on the board as pupils arrive: two from yesterday, two from last week, one from last month. Answers on paper, self-checked, a show of results for each. When the last-month question is right in six books out of thirty, that topic goes back on next week's plan.
notice: Which time horizon fails first: yesterday's content, last week's or last month's.
Whether the results ever change your plan. A review that never alters the pace has become a ritual.
Which pupils are consistently caught out only by the older material.
consider: Little means little. Ten minutes that grow into twenty crowd out the teaching the review exists to serve.
Keep the stakes low. The information dries up as soon as the review starts to feel like a test.
pages.wider: The daily, weekly and monthly review pattern comes from Rosenshine's principles of instruction, distilled from observation of the most effective classrooms.

why: Re-reading notes feels productive because the material becomes familiar, and familiarity imitates knowing. Self quizzing feels worse and works better; in the card's words, retrieval effort drives long term memory.
Teaching pupils to quiz themselves passes on the strand's whole machinery. The checking that has been happening in your lessons becomes something they can run without you.
example: A teacher demonstrates a revision cycle: cover the notes, write everything you can recall about the topic, check against the notes, and mark the gaps as the material to return to in a few days. Pupils practise the cycle in class, on content from a fortnight ago, before being asked to use it at home.
pages.try: Teach the cover, write, check cycle explicitly in one lesson. The moment where pupils check and find their gaps is the part to make visible, because that is the moment re-reading never provides.
notice: Which pupils revert to re-reading when unsupervised. The pull of the easier strategy is strong precisely because it feels like progress.
Whether self quizzing turns up in how pupils talk about their revision, not just in the lesson where you taught it.
consider: The spaced part needs as much teaching as the quizzing. Returning to material after days rather than minutes is what the card's title is carrying, and it is the half pupils are most likely to drop.
pages.wider: Bjork's research underpins both halves of this card: retrieval as a desirable difficulty, and learners' unreliable instincts about which study strategies actually work.

why: Hours of marking can produce no feedback at all. If a pupil never reads or acts on your comments, you have marked the work but nothing has been fed back. No engagement, no feedback.

The distinction changes where the effort goes. Marking is finished when the pen goes down; feedback is finished when the pupil has done something because of it. So the engagement has to be planned before the work goes back, not hoped for afterwards.
example: A history teacher returning essays plans the first ten minutes of the next lesson before writing a single comment: pupils will reread their feedback, rewrite one sentence in response, and be ready to say what their comment asked of them. The comments then get written knowing exactly how they will be used.
pages.try: Before you mark your next set, decide what pupils will do with the comments and when. If you cannot find that time, mark less and protect it.
notice: Whether pupils read comments unprompted or wait to be told to.
How many of your comments lead to a visible change in the work.
How long the engagement takes compared with how long the marking took.
consider: Engagement needs lesson time, which means something else gives way. That trade-off is a planning decision, not an afterthought.
A comment written for a pupil to act on reads differently from a comment written to show the work was marked. It helps to know which one you are writing.
tech: Audio comments and digital ink can shorten the gap between work and response to almost nothing, and feedback that arrives while the work is still fresh has a far better chance of shaping what pupils do next. The tool does not change the rule, though: a recorded comment nobody listens to is still marking, not feedback. If you use the approved audio or annotation tool in your setting, plan the listening and the response with the same care as the recording.
pages.wider: This sits squarely in Wiliam's account of formative assessment, in which comments and evidence only count for anything once they change what the learner does next.

why: Most comments tell a pupil how they did and stop there. Hattie and Timperley's three questions, where am I going, how am I doing, what next, are a quick test of whether a comment can actually move the work on.

A comment that only answers the second question leaves the pupil holding a judgement with nowhere to take it. The first question needs shared criteria; the third needs a next step the pupil can act on.
example: A science teacher marking investigation write-ups checks each comment against the three questions before handing back. Where a comment reads only as a verdict, she adds a line naming the goal and a line naming the next move: your conclusion describes the pattern, the criteria ask you to explain it, so use your graph to say why it happens.
pages.try: Take the last five comments you wrote and sort them against the three questions. If the middle column fills fastest, you know what to add next time.
notice: Whether pupils can tell you their next step after reading your comment, in their own words.
Which of the three questions your comments favour across a whole set.
consider: Where am I going only functions when criteria have been shared and understood first, which is Sadler's territory as much as this card's.
What next needs time to act built in, or the third question gets answered and then wasted.
pages.wider: Hattie and Timperley's review found feedback to be among the most powerful influences on achievement and among the most variable; the three questions are their account of the difference.

why: Not all comments do the same job. Hattie and Timperley distinguish feedback aimed at the task, at the process the pupil used, and at the person, and the levels are not equally useful: task and process feedback improve learning, while praise aimed at the self undermines it.
Naming your target before you write is a small discipline with a large effect on what ends up on the page. A comment about the person is usually easy to spot once you start looking for it.
example: Marking a set of maths books, a teacher catches himself about to write that a pupil is a natural at this, and replaces it with a process comment: checking your answer against an estimate is what caught the error here. Same warmth, different target.
pages.try: For one class set, label each comment T, P or S as you write it: task, process or self. The labels are for you, not the pupils.
notice: How much of your praise, when labelled honestly, turns out to be aimed at the person.
Whether pupils can say what a comment was about: the answer, the method, or them.
consider: Warmth belongs in the classroom; it just should not be doing the job of feedback on the learning. The two can live in the same conversation without living in the same sentence.
pages.wider: The levels come from Hattie and Timperley's model of feedback, and their warning about self-level praise is echoed independently in Kluger and DeNisi's findings on feedback that draws attention to the self.

why: Kluger and DeNisi's finding is one of the most sobering in this strand: over a third of feedback interventions made performance worse. Feedback is powerful, but the power runs in both directions.

The dividing line in their analysis is where attention goes. Comments that keep a pupil's attention on the work tend to help; comments that pull attention to the self tend not to. The check on the card, work or student, is the practical version of that finding.
example: Before returning books, a languages teacher reads her own comments as if she were the pupil receiving them. Two turn out to be about the pupil rather than the translation in front of them; both get rewritten to name something in the work: this tense is the one to fix, these five words need the accent check you used above.
notice: How pupils respond in the moment work is returned: heads down into the work, or looking around comparing themselves with others.
Which of your comments you would be glad to receive about your own work.
consider: A comment can be about the student without naming them. Try harder, more effort needed and you can do better are all self-directed, whatever the phrasing.
pages.wider: As the strand's opening argument puts it, some feedback helps, some does very little, and some makes things worse; Kluger and DeNisi supplied the numbers behind that sentence.

why: Before feedback can do anything, three conditions have to hold. Sadler's argument, which anchors much of this strand, is that pupils must know what quality looks like, be able to compare their own work against it, and have the chance to close the gap they find.

Miss any one and the rest stalls. Criteria shared after the work is finished cannot guide it; a comparison pupils cannot make wastes the criteria; a gap identified with no time to close it just sits there.
example: Before a design and technology project begins, the class examines the criteria alongside two finished products of different quality and discusses which criteria separate them. Halfway through making, pupils stop and place their own work against the same criteria before deciding what to do next.
pages.try: Check one upcoming task against the three conditions: criteria shared first, a built-in moment to compare, time to act on what the comparison shows. Add whichever is missing before changing anything else.
notice: Whether pupils' judgements of their own work start to resemble yours, which is the comparison condition beginning to function.
Which of the three conditions your current routine handles least well.
consider: Criteria pupils have never seen exemplified tend to stay abstract. Showing what quality looks like in real work can do more than a list of statements alone.
The three conditions are a design test as much as a marking one: they can be checked before a task is set, not just afterwards.
pages.wider: Sadler's conditions are the hinge of this strand, and Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick built directly on them, placing feedback within pupils' growing ability to judge and improve their own work.

why: Some errors should not be left to sit. On simple and procedural tasks, Shute found that quick feedback stops mistakes embedding; every repetition of a wrong method is practice at being wrong.
Waiting until next lesson to fix what could be fixed now hands the error a week of rehearsal.
example: During column subtraction practice, a teacher checks answers as pupils work rather than collecting books in. A pupil subtracting the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position is caught on question three, not question thirty.
pages.try: Pick one procedural practice task this week and mark it live, in the room, instead of taking it away. Books stay open; errors get fixed at the desk.
notice: Whether the same procedural errors reappear later in the week, which is the test of whether the correction landed.
What pupils do immediately after a correction: redo the question, or move straight on.
consider: Immediate correction is for the simple and procedural. On complex work the guide's advice runs the other way: let the struggle do its work first.
Deciding which tasks count as simple is a judgement about your class and your subject. The teacher in the room knows, not a website.
tech: An approved auto-marked quiz or response tool in your setting can give every pupil that immediate correction at once, which no teacher circulating a room can match for procedural practice. The trap named in this strand still applies: a score, a tick or a badge that stops there is information, not feedback. Build in the moment where pupils redo the questions they got wrong, or the speed achieves nothing.
pages.wider: Shute's review of formative feedback is the source here: timing is not a matter of taste but of task, with quick correction suited to simple work.

why: Speed is not always a virtue. On complex work, the research Shute and Kulhavy report points to a short delay before feedback, because immediate correction can short-circuit the very thinking the task was set to provoke.
A pupil midway through wrestling with a hard problem does not need the answer arriving; they need the wrestle. Feedback that lands too early can turn a thinking task into a copying one.
example: After pupils attempt a multi-step physics problem, the teacher collects the attempts and says nothing that lesson. Feedback comes at the start of the next one, once pupils have some distance from their own reasoning, and begins by asking them to name their sticking point before they read the comment.
pages.try: Choose one genuinely complex task and deliberately hold your feedback for a day. Notice what you would have interrupted.
notice: Whether pupils persist longer when they know correction is not imminent.
What pupils ask you during the task when they cannot hand the struggle straight back to you.
consider: This card and Immediate for Simple Tasks are one principle, not two: match timing to task complexity. Which is which is a judgement for the teacher who knows the class and the content.
Delay is short. A day or a lesson lets processing happen; two weeks is just slow marking.
pages.wider: Shute's review and Kulhavy's earlier work both found that feedback timing interacts with task difficulty; there is no single right speed, only a right speed for this task.

why: Feedback returned weeks after the work is a post-mortem: accurate, perhaps, but too late to change anything. Feedback given while pupils are still working shapes the work itself, which is the formative case Black and Wiliam made.
Proximity is strategy. Moving around the room during the task puts you where feedback is cheapest and most usable: at the point of the error, in the moment it happens.
example: While pupils draft persuasive letters, the teacher circulates on a deliberate route rather than answering hands. Reading over shoulders, she catches the same weak opening in four books and pauses the room for ninety seconds to address it before it spreads further.
pages.try: In your next extended task, plan your route around the room the way you would plan a question: who you will reach first, and what you are looking for when you arrive.
notice: How many errors you catch mid-task that would otherwise have travelled home in thirty books.
Which pupils you naturally reach and which you consistently miss. A deliberate route usually exposes a pattern.
consider: Intervening in the moment suits some errors and not others; on complex thinking the guide advises letting the struggle run first. In-the-moment feedback is a timing choice, not a default.
pages.wider: This is Black and Wiliam's central argument in practical form: assessment is formative only when it adjusts teaching and learning while the learning is still underway.

why: Butler's study gives this strand one of its clearest warnings: when a grade sits alongside a comment, pupils look at the grade and miss the guidance. Comments alone produced the greatest gains.
The grade does not just distract from the comment, it cancels it. Two lines of careful writing in the margin cannot compete with a number at the top of the page.
example: A geography teacher returns assessed work with comments only. Pupils respond to the comments and improve one section; only then, at the end of the week, do the grades go into the gradebook and become visible.
pages.try: Choose one low-stakes piece and return it comment-only. Compare what pupils do with it against what they did last time a grade was attached.
notice: The first thing pupils look for when work comes back, and how long they spend on the words once there is no number to find.
Whether the talk between pupils shifts from comparing scores to comparing responses.
consider: If your school mandates grades, the card's advice is sequencing, not defiance: delay the grade until the feedback has been used.
Comment-only work still needs comments worth acting on. Removing the grade exposes the quality of what is left.
tech: Most digital gradebooks and annotation tools show pupils a score the moment work is returned, which puts Butler's problem straight back on screen. If the approved tool in your setting has a hide-grades or scheduled-release option, use it: comments first, response time next, the number afterwards.
pages.wider: Butler's research distinguished task-involving from ego-involving feedback; a grade pulls attention towards how I did as a person, which is precisely the attention shift Kluger and DeNisi found so costly.

why: A page of comments overwhelms the pupil and exhausts the teacher, and much of it goes unread. The evidence in this guide is blunt about that: feedback is not what the teacher gives, it is what the learner does with it, and nobody does thirty things with thirty comments.
One or two precise targets land. Choosing them is harder than writing many, because it forces the judgement about what would make the biggest difference to this pupil right now.
example: Marking a set of essays, a teacher writes one sentence per script: the single change that would most improve the next draft. Marking gets noticeably quicker, but the real change comes next lesson: ten minutes acting on the target, and for once every pupil knows exactly what theirs is.
pages.try: Mark your next class set with a one-target rule. If you catch yourself writing a second comment, ask whether it matters more than the first; if it does, swap them.
notice: Whether pupils can tell you their target the next day. With a page of comments they usually cannot; with one they usually can.
What happens to the quality of your chosen targets when choosing is the whole job.
consider: Less volume only works alongside time to act. One precise target that pupils never get a lesson minute to address is still wasted effort.
This is about work in progress. Summative points where fuller commentary is required are a different job.
pages.wider: Kluger and DeNisi's meta-analysis found over a third of feedback interventions made performance worse; precision and focus are much of what separates the feedback that helps.
tech: A digital highlight or pin tool, the approved one in your setting, suits this well: one marked spot, one comment, nothing else competing for attention. Audio comments can carry the single target quickly too. Faster feedback only matters if pupils use it.

why: Handing assessment over to pupils without structure produces what Topping's research predicts: empty praise, vague niceness, the occasional unkindness. With criteria and a protocol, peer feedback becomes learning for both the giver and the receiver.
There is a second benefit hiding in it. Judging another pupil's work against criteria is practice at the very comparison Sadler says pupils must learn to make about their own.
example: Pupils swap lab reports with a fixed protocol: check the report against two named criteria, mark where each is met, and write one question for the author. No general comments allowed. The teacher then samples the peer feedback itself, because the quality of the judging is evidence too.
pages.try: Start with one criterion, not a rubric. Pupils check a partner's work against a single shared criterion and mark exactly where it is or is not met.
notice: The language pupils use about work: criteria words appearing in their talk is the structure doing its job.
Whether feedback stays on the work or drifts to the person, which pupils find as hard as adults do.
consider: The protocol carries the strategy. Without it the activity tends to revert to swap-and-be-nice within a lesson or two.
Pupils need feedback literacy before they can give feedback, not just receive it. Modelling what a useful peer comment looks like is worth doing at least once first.
pages.wider: Topping's work on peer assessment found benefits flowing to assessor and assessed alike, provided the structure holds; the structure is not optional scaffolding but the mechanism itself.

why: Andrade's finding rearranges the usual worry about self-assessment. Pupils' judgements do not need to be accurate for the practice to work; it is the act of comparing work against criteria that improves performance. Process is the point.

That takes the pressure off. You are not training examiners; you are giving pupils repeated practice at holding their work up against a standard, which is exactly the comparison Sadler's conditions require.
example: Before handing in an essay, pupils complete a short self-review against the criteria: where each is met, where it is not, and one change made as a result. The teacher marks the essay afterwards as usual, but reads the self-review first.
pages.try: Add one line to your submission routine: before this comes to me, mark the place where you best meet the criteria and the place where you least do.
notice: Whether pupils' self-judgements move closer to yours over a term. Accuracy is not the goal, but drift towards it suggests the comparing is genuine.
What pupils change between self-review and submission. A self-assessment that changes nothing was a form-filling exercise.
consider: Self-assessment against criteria pupils do not understand is guesswork. Sadler's first condition, knowing what quality looks like, comes before this card, not after it.
pages.wider: Andrade's research sits within the self-regulation tradition of Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick and Boud: feedback practices that build the pupil's own evaluative judgement, not just improve the next piece of work.

why: A written comment is usually a full stop. Carless's research argues for making it a turn in a conversation instead: pupils question, clarify and respond to comments over time rather than receiving a final judgement.
Uptake rises when feedback works this way, partly because a pupil who can ask what a comment means no longer has to guess, and a pupil who has replied to a comment has already begun to act on it.
example: A teacher returns draft coursework with two margin comments each, one ending in a question. Pupils reply in writing before redrafting, and the teacher answers the replies rather than writing fresh comments, so each piece carries a short thread of exchange rather than a verdict.
pages.try: End one comment per pupil with a question that needs an answer, and collect the answers. The replies show you which comments were understood.
notice: Which comments generate genuine replies and which get token ones; the difference maps closely onto which comments were worth writing.
Whether pupils start initiating. Asking about a comment is feedback literacy showing itself.
consider: Dialogue takes longer than delivery, so it cannot be every piece. Choosing where a feedback conversation pays its way, usually a draft heading for redraft rather than a finished piece, is the design decision.
pages.wider: Carless's work on feedback uptake, alongside Boud's on learner capacity, points the same way: pupils act on feedback they have had a hand in making sense of.

why: Not every kind of feedback needs you. Automated tools can check factual accuracy and procedural correctness faster than any teacher; what they cannot do is respond to voice, argument or creativity. The card's advice is a division of labour: match the feedback source to what is being assessed.
Done well, this buys back the scarcest resource in the system, teacher attention, and spends it where automation cannot go.
example: In a languages classroom, the approved practice tool handles vocabulary and conjugation accuracy, correcting as pupils go. The teacher's written feedback on the same unit leaves those layers alone and addresses how convincingly the pupil's letter argues its case.
pages.try: List what you marked in your last set, then sort it: accuracy and correctness on one side, voice, argument and quality of thinking on the other. Ask what on the first list a tool in your setting could carry.
notice: Whether your own comments become fewer and more substantial once accuracy checking moves elsewhere.
Whether pupils act on automated corrections or click past them. A tick accepted without a redo has fed nothing back.
consider: The strand's warning applies with full force here: automated feedback that gives a score, a tick or a badge and stops there is information, not feedback. The tool supplies the correction; you still supply the time and the expectation that pupils use it.
tech: The card's own framing is the safeguard. Use the approved adaptive or AI-assisted tool in your setting for what it is designed to assess, factual accuracy and procedural correctness, and reserve yourself for the rest; judgements about argument, voice and creativity stay with you. The question to keep asking is not whether the tool's feedback is fast, which it will be, but whether pupils do anything with it. Speed only counts when it leads to a correction, a retry or a redraft.
pages.wider: Shute's review supports quick, automated correction for procedural work, while Black and Wiliam's account of formative practice describes what no tool replaces: the professional judgement about where the learning goes next.

why: Reading a class set reveals things no single script can: the same misconception in eleven books, a strength half the class shares, one gap that would repay whole-class teaching. Whole class feedback works from those patterns. Teach to the gap, not to each paper.
It is sustainable for you and precise for pupils, a rare combination in feedback. Thirty individual paragraphs saying the same thing serve nobody better than one well-taught response to the pattern.
example: After reading a set of essays without writing in them, a teacher notes three recurring issues and one common strength. Next lesson opens with the pattern: what this class does well, the error many share, the one improvement to make now. Pupils then find and fix that issue in their own work.
pages.try: Read your next set with a blank sheet beside you and nothing in your pen for the books. Record patterns only, and build the follow-up lesson from the sheet.
notice: Whether pupils can locate the general point in their own work, which is the step where whole class feedback succeeds or fails.
How your reading changes when you are hunting patterns rather than composing comments.
consider: Some pupils will need the bridge built for them: the class-level point and their own page are not automatically connected. A quick check on who has found their own example is worth the two minutes.
Whole class feedback replaces some individual marking, not all of it. Which pieces still need an individual response is a judgement about the work and the class.
tech: A shared display or class document is where the patterns become teachable: common strengths and errors laid out once, visible to everyone, annotated live as the class works through them. Kept in the approved shared space in your setting, the same document becomes a running record of what this class has been taught to fix, which is useful the next time a pattern threatens to return.
pages.wider: This is Wiliam's formative logic applied at class scale, and it reflects Hattie and Timperley's point that feedback informs the teacher as much as the taught: the set tells you what to do next.

why: The fastest way to make feedback backfire is to aim it at the person. Kluger and DeNisi found that comments threatening self-concept decrease performance; attention pulled to the self is attention pulled off the work.
The card's two examples carry the rule. This paragraph needs restructuring gives the pupil somewhere to go. You need to try harder gives them somewhere to hide.
example: Rereading his comments before returning books, a teacher rewrites each one whose subject is the pupil until its subject is the work: you have not explained this becomes this step needs the reason it works, and you must check your work becomes three of these answers fail the estimate test.
pages.try: Scan your last set of comments for sentences whose subject is the pupil. Rewrite each so the subject is a specific piece of the work.
notice: Whether returned work produces defensiveness or redrafting; the difference often follows where the comments were aimed.
Which pupils you most often address person-first. It may be exactly the ones for whom work-directed comments would help most.
consider: Task-directed does not mean cold. The warmth can live in the conversation while the written feedback stays on the work.
pages.wider: Kluger and DeNisi's analysis holds that the closer feedback moves to the self, the less useful it becomes; Hattie and Timperley's levels tell the same story from a different dataset.

why: If a comment asks nothing of the pupil, it is information, not feedback. Wiliam's test is demanding: the measure of feedback is the thinking it causes, and a comment that does the pupil's thinking for them causes none.
Why might this be stronger with evidence leaves work for the learner. Inserting the evidence yourself finishes the job and ends the learning.
example: A computing teacher stops writing the fix beside broken code. Instead each comment names the symptom and asks a question: this loop never ends, so what condition would stop it? Pupils write the answer, then make the change.
pages.try: Before returning your next set, reread each comment asking one question: what will the pupil have to think about to use this? If the answer is nothing, rewrite it.
notice: How long pupils spend with returned work. Comments that cause thinking take visible time to act on.
The quality of what pupils produce in response. A poor response often reveals a comment that told rather than asked.
consider: Causing thinking presupposes time to think. This card fails without lesson minutes set aside for the response.
Not every comment needs to be a puzzle. Simple procedural slips are better corrected than pondered; save the thinking for where thinking pays.
pages.wider: This is Wiliam's contribution to the strand distilled: feedback exists to change the learner's thinking, and anything that bypasses the thinking bypasses the learning.

why: Praise feels safe, and that is exactly why it needs care. Butler found task-involving feedback improves performance while ego-involving feedback shifts attention from the learning to the self-image, and praise of traits, cleverness, talent, being a natural, is ego-involving however kindly meant.
Praise the strategy and the praise becomes reusable: a pupil told their method worked can use that method again. A pupil told they are gifted has nothing to act on.
example: A music teacher watching a pupil finally manage a difficult passage says: slowing it right down and only speeding up when it was clean, that is what got you there. The praise names something the pupil chose to do and can choose again.
pages.try: For a week, make every piece of praise name a decision the pupil made. If you cannot find the decision, watch longer before praising.
notice: Whether praised strategies get reused, by the pupil praised and by those listening.
What happens to pupils' willingness to attempt hard tasks when praise attaches to methods rather than ability.
consider: This is a phrasing habit more than a policy, and habits shift slowly. A short list of strategy-praise stems kept where you can see it, for you rather than the pupils, does the early lifting.
pages.wider: Butler's task- and ego-involvement distinction converges with Kluger and DeNisi's meta-analysis: feedback that turns attention to the self, praise included, tends to cost performance rather than raise it.

why: Pupils are rarely taught how to read feedback, and it shows. A comment that seems transparent to the teacher who wrote it can be opaque to the pupil holding it, and acting on feedback is a skill with steps: understand the comment, locate it in the work, know the move it asks for.
Carless and Boud call this feedback literacy, and their point is on the card: it is taught, not assumed.
example: Before returning the first marked piece of the year, a teacher puts one of her own typical comments on the board and walks through it: here is what it says, here is what it means, here is what I would do in response. Pupils then decode one of their own comments in pairs before acting alone.
pages.try: Take the card's own script into your next return-of-work lesson: one comment, modelled aloud, meaning and next move included, before pupils touch their own.
notice: The questions pupils ask about comments. Fewer what-does-this-mean questions over a term is the literacy building.
Whether the modelling transfers: can pupils decode a comment shaped differently from the one you modelled?
consider: Literacy is easier to build when there is a consistent shape to read. If your comments follow a predictable pattern, pupils can learn that pattern; comments written differently every time keep them beginners.
pages.wider: Feedback literacy is Carless and Boud's term for the learner's side of the exchange: the capacity to understand, evaluate and use what comes back, without which the teacher's side achieves little.

why: Sometimes the most useful move is an audit rather than a new strategy. Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's seven principles offer the checklist: do you clarify criteria, enable self-assessment, encourage dialogue, help close the gap? The card's instruction is direct: redesign where you do not.

The card names four of the principles as its worked examples; the full seven are worth having to hand for the audit. Good feedback practice clarifies what good performance looks like, develops self-assessment and reflection, delivers high quality information to pupils about their learning, encourages dialogue around learning with teachers and peers, encourages positive motivational beliefs, provides opportunities to close the gap between current and desired performance, and gives teachers information they can use to shape their teaching.

Their deeper argument, picked up throughout this strand, is that feedback belongs inside self-regulation. Its job is to make pupils better at judging and improving their own work, not more dependent on yours.
example: A teacher audits one unit against the principles and finds two absences: pupils never self-assess before submitting, and no comment ever gets a reply. She changes only those two things for the next unit and leaves what already works alone.
notice: Which principles your practice already covers without ever having named them, and which are absent entirely.
Whether the redesigns hold once the unit is underway, or fall away under time pressure. What falls first shows you what to protect.
consider: An audit of everything changes nothing. One unit, honestly examined, beats a whole curriculum skimmed.
pages.wider: Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick built on Sadler's foundations, reframing feedback around the pupil's growing power of self-regulation; the seven principles are that argument in usable form.

why: Time to act is the part most often squeezed out, and the strand is blunt about the cost: feedback with no time to act on it is wasted. Every hour of marking is spent or lost in the ten minutes after work is returned.

Beginning the next lesson with pupils reading and responding to comments before anything new makes the priority structural rather than aspirational. The response is the learning event; the comments were only ever preparation for it.
example: Work goes back at the start of the lesson, not the end. Pupils read their comments, rewrite one section in response, and only then does new content begin. Nothing about the routine is complicated; its value is that it happens every time work is returned.
pages.try: Protect the first ten minutes after any returned work for responding to it. Put it in your planning as a fixed cost of setting the work in the first place.
notice: What pupils produce in the response window. The redrafts are better evidence of your feedback's quality than the comments themselves.
Whether pupils begin expecting the routine and arrive ready to respond. Expectation is the habit forming.
consider: If there is genuinely no time for pupils to act, the honest options are to mark less or reclaim the time. Writing comments that will never be used is the one option the evidence rules out.
tech: Sharing feedback through the approved platform in your setting the evening before, as the card suggests, moves the reading out of the lesson so that lesson time goes entirely on the response. The strand's closing line is the test to hold onto: the win is not faster feedback, the win is better work because pupils had time to use it.
pages.wider: Wiliam and Leahy's practical work on embedding formative assessment treats the response to feedback as a planned classroom routine, not a hope; this card is that principle in its simplest form.

why: When you correct a pupil's work for them, you do the thinking and they watch. Returning work with questions instead keeps the cognitive work where the learning is: with the pupil.
What evidence supports this claim? demands something of the writer that inserting the missing evidence never will. If feedback requires no response from the learner, it is information, not feedback.
example: An English teacher returns paragraphs with a margin question each: which word here tells the reader how to feel, or what is your evidence for this? The lesson opens with pupils answering their question in a different colour before any new content begins.
pages.try: On the next piece you mark, replace the corrections on one section with questions, and give five minutes next lesson for written answers. The answers will tell you whether the questions were any good.
notice: The quality of pupils' responses. A question that gets a one-word answer back was probably a correction wearing a question mark.
Whether the same question stops being needed over time, which is the point of asking rather than fixing.
consider: Simple procedural slips are often better corrected immediately; the guide is clear that quick feedback stops mistakes embedding on simple tasks. Save the questions for the thinking, not the typos.
Pupils need to know how to act on a question, which is feedback literacy and has to be taught with an exemplar at least once.
pages.wider: This is Hattie and Timperley's territory: feedback that works answers where next, and a good question is often the most honest form that answer can take.
tech: An annotation tool with a reply function, through your setting's approved platform, turns each margin question into a visible exchange: your question, their written answer, in one place. The reply is the point; a question with nowhere to answer it is a correction in disguise.

why: Boud's argument reaches past the next piece of work. If pupils always need you to tell them how they did, the system has failed, however good the telling; feedback should be building the learner's capacity to judge quality for themselves.

That reframes the goal of much of this strand. Criteria, self-assessment, dialogue and time to act are not only ways to improve this essay; they are an apprenticeship in judging quality, and an apprenticeship is supposed to end.
example: Across a term, pupils build a portfolio in which every submitted piece carries their own prior judgement against the criteria. The teacher's response engages with the judgement as much as the work: where the pupil's assessment was sound, it says so and steps back; where it missed, that gap becomes the feedback.
pages.try: Before your next round of marking, ask pupils to predict the feedback they will get. Your marking then confirms, refines or corrects their judgement, which is the capacity you are trying to build.
notice: Whether pupils' predictions of their feedback sharpen over time.
Who still cannot start work without asking whether it is right, and whether that number falls.
consider: Independence is designed in gradually, not declared. The scaffolds of criteria and structured self-review come first and fade later; how fast to fade them is a judgement about the class in front of you.
pages.wider: Boud's case for sustainable feedback extends Sadler's conditions and Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick's self-regulation principles to their logical end: feedback that gradually makes itself unnecessary.

why: Good feedback rarely happens by accident, and the closing card of the strand says why: feedback designed into learning from the start works; left to chance, it does not. Who gives it, when, in what form, and when pupils act on it are scheme-of-work decisions, not marking-night improvisations.

Designing it in also makes the rest of the strand affordable. Comment-only pieces, peer review, whole class feedback and response time stop competing for lesson minutes when the scheme already holds a place for each.
example: Planning a six-week unit, a teacher fixes two feedback points before sequencing any content: a mid-unit draft that gets whole class feedback with a response lesson, and a final piece that gets individual comments with time to act. Everything else in the unit is arranged around those fixed points.
pages.try: Open your next unit plan and look for the moment pupils act on feedback. If you cannot point to it, add it before adding anything else.
notice: How the designed feedback points survive contact with the term. What gets skipped under pressure shows where the design needs protecting, or rethinking.
Whether pupils know the rhythm: when feedback is coming and what they will be expected to do with it.
consider: Design includes deciding what will not get detailed feedback. A scheme that promises rich feedback on everything is unlikely to deliver it on anything.
pages.wider: Sadler's conditions, Carless's dialogue and Boud's sustainability all describe systems rather than moments, and this card draws the conclusion: feedback is a feature of curriculum design, not an event that follows it.

why: Anderson and Krathwohl give you a map of what a question asks a learner to do: remembering, understanding, applying, analysing, evaluating, creating. Without a map like this, questioning tends to settle into one register, and classroom talk becomes thinner than the thinking you want.

The card's caution is as important as the taxonomy itself: these are not a hierarchy of worth. Recall is foundational, not inferior, and a lesson full of analysis questions built on insecure knowledge helps nobody.
example: A history teacher looks back across a fortnight of questions on the causes of the First World War. What year, which countries: remembering. Why did the alliance system raise the stakes: analysing. Was any single country most responsible: evaluating. Nothing about the teaching changes yet; what changes is that the teacher can now see which kinds of thinking are being asked for, and which never are.
pages.try: Write down the questions you asked in one lesson, from memory or from your slides, and place each against the six levels. The spread, or the lack of it, is the finding.
notice: Which levels dominate across a week, and which never appear.
Whether recall questions are doing their foundational work before you ask for analysis or evaluation.
What happens to answers when you deliberately ask at a level you rarely use.
consider: The taxonomy is a map, not a ladder to be climbed in every lesson. Which level a class needs next is a judgement about their knowledge, and that judgement is yours.
This pairs naturally with planning questions before the lesson; the levels are most useful before the room fills up.
pages.wider: Anderson and Krathwohl's revision of the taxonomy is one of the most widely used frameworks for question design; their insistence that recall is foundational, not inferior, is the part most often forgotten.

why: Not every good question suits every moment. Hattie and Zierer distinguish surface questions that establish what, deep questions that probe why, and transfer questions that ask where else this applies. Each serves a different stage of learning.

The failure mode is reaching for transfer too early. Asking students to apply a concept elsewhere before the surface knowledge is secure sets them up to fail, and the failure can look like inability when it is really sequencing.
example: Early in a unit on electricity: what are the components of this circuit? Once that is secure: why does the bulb dim when a second one is added? Later still: where else does the idea of sharing a limited supply appear? Same topic, three stages, three kinds of question.
pages.try: Before writing the key questions for your next lesson, ask one question of yourself first: what stage is this class at with this content?
notice: How students handle why questions. Struggle there often signals that the surface layer is not yet secure.
Whether discussion changes when the question matches the stage rather than the scheme of work's ambitions.
consider: Stage is about this class and this content now, not about ability. The same lesson can hold students at different stages, and only you can see where each one is.
Surface questions are not lesser questions. The previous card makes the same point about recall; the two frameworks agree.
pages.wider: The surface, deep and transfer model comes from Hattie and Zierer's synthesis of how learning moves through phases, each with its own kind of question.

why: Most classroom questions have a destination the teacher already holds, and students know it. Dillon found that genuine open questions, the ones where the teacher does not know the answer, produce the most extended student reasoning.
That is a different thing from a closed question in open clothing. Guess what I am thinking is a game, not an enquiry, and students play it efficiently rather than thoughtfully.
example: An English teacher asks which character in the novel changes most, genuinely undecided herself. Students take different positions, and because there is no answer to converge on, they have to argue from the text. The discussion runs longer than planned and does not resolve, which is fine.
pages.try: Plan one genuinely open question into next week: one where you would find it hard to say what a right answer looks like.
notice: The length of the reasoning compared with your closed questions, which is what Dillon measured.
Whether students begin addressing each other rather than routing everything through you.
Your own urge to steer the room towards a view you privately hold.
consider: Not every question needs a predetermined destination, but many still will. Open questions do their work partly because they are occasional and genuine, not the default.
An open question still needs something to reason with. A class without secure knowledge of the novel cannot argue about it.
tech: A shared whiteboard or discussion board from your school's approved set can hold the range of positions an open question produces, and it keeps the reasoning there to return to in a later lesson, so a useful conversation is not lost the moment the lesson moves on. It can also bring in students who would not venture an unfinished idea aloud; the thinking still has to be theirs.
pages.wider: Dillon's studies of questioning are unusual for how sceptical they are about questions themselves; this card and its neighbour on alternatives both come from that scepticism.

why: Questions asked on the spur of the moment default to recall. The card is precise about why: not because recall is wrong but because planning stops there. In the flow of a lesson, the question that comes to mind is the one that is easiest to form.
Writing questions before the lesson, at every level of Anderson and Krathwohl's taxonomy, turns the framework from a poster into a planning tool.
example: Planning a lesson on rivers, a geography teacher writes six questions into the slides in advance, from what is erosion through to how would you defend this village, and why there. In the lesson the questions are simply ready, instead of needing to be invented mid-explanation.
pages.try: For one lesson this week, write three questions in advance at levels you know you would not improvise. Put them where you will see them.
notice: The difference in students' answers between your planned questions and your improvised ones.
Which planned questions you actually asked. The ones that never got used tell you something about the lesson's shape.
consider: Plan the pivotal questions, not a script. The point is to have the harder questions ready, not to close down where the discussion goes.
Improvised questions keep their place; responsiveness is part of the craft. Planning removes the ceiling, it does not remove the improvising.

stair.lede: Drafting a ladder of questions across the levels is planning work AI can accelerate, through the approved tool in your setting, with the framework the card names built into the prompt:
stair.prompt:
Act as a secondary English teacher. Create a set of questions on the poem I am teaching to Year 10, one question at each of these levels: remembering, understanding, applying, analysing, evaluating, creating.

Label each question with its level. Keep every question concise and answerable in discussion, not as an essay task.

Do not include answers, model responses or commentary.

[paste the poem or topic details here]
stair.after: The levels are a planning tool, not a hierarchy of worth: recall is foundational, not inferior. Draft with the tool, then choose and reorder for your class. Iterate until the ladder fits the lesson you're actually teaching.

pages.wider: This is Anderson and Krathwohl put to work: the taxonomy read not as a description of questions but as a discipline for writing them.
tech: A lesson planning or slide tool keeps planned questions where you'll actually use them. The planning is the strategy; the tool just stores it.

why: Dillon's finding runs against instinct: statements and silence often elicit richer responses than questions do. A steady stream of questions can turn discussion into interrogation, with the teacher's voice as the engine and every exchange routed through the front.

Tell me more. I had not considered that. These hand the floor back without demanding a particular answer, and the card's own summary is the one to remember: not every probe needs to end with a question mark.
example: In a discussion of a moral question in RE, a pupil offers a view. The teacher says, I had not considered that, and stops. The pupil keeps going, and a second pupil responds to the first rather than waiting for the next question.
notice: What follows a statement compared with what follows a question.
How many questions you ask in ten minutes of discussion; counting is revealing in itself.
Whether pupils begin responding to each other when you probe less.
consider: Silence is one of Dillon's alternatives too, which makes wait time the natural companion to this card.
Statements work when they are genuine. I had not considered that only lands if you actually had not.
pages.wider: Dillon spent a career questioning the primacy of questions; his alternatives are the practical residue of that work.

why: Mary Budd Rowe timed teachers waiting after their questions and found most give less than a second before speaking again: rephrasing, prompting, or answering themselves. Under a second is not thinking time for anyone.
Extending the pause to three seconds costs nothing, needs no resources, and changes the answers. Silence after a question is not dead air; it is where better thinking often begins.
example: A teacher asks why the character makes the choice she does, then counts three in their head. The silence feels far longer from the front than it does from the desks. The first answer that comes is a sentence rather than a word, and a second pupil builds on it unprompted.
pages.try: Pick one lesson and hold three seconds after every substantive question. Counting silently is not a gimmick; the urge to fill the gap is strong enough to need a mechanism.
notice: The length and complexity of answers, which is exactly what Rowe measured improving.
Who answers. The extra seconds bring in pupils who compose before speaking and were always beaten to it.
Your own discomfort. It fades with practice, and it is the price of the better answers.
consider: The pause after a pupil answers matters too, and is its own strategy; the pair are stronger together.
Three seconds of silence only helps in a room where a slow answer is safe. If cold calling feels threatening in your class, the climate work comes first.
pages.wider: Rowe's wait time studies are the origin; her line that slowing down may be a way of speeding up is still the best one-sentence case for it.

why: Rowe identified a second wait time that gets far less attention than the first: the pause after a student responds. Held for three seconds, it prompts elaboration and self-correction that an immediate teacher response cuts off.
Silence after an answer signals that more is expected. Respond instantly, even warmly, and the thinking stops there.
example: A pupil explains why the graph flattens, and stops. The teacher says nothing and holds the silence for three seconds. The pupil adds the condition they had missed, unprompted, and corrects their own units on the way.
pages.try: Run both wait times together for a lesson: three seconds after you ask, three seconds after they answer. The second pause is the harder habit, because an answer feels like your cue.
notice: Self-corrections you did not have to make for them.
Whether answers grow past their first full stop.
Whether other pupils come in during the pause without being asked.
consider: After a wrong answer, the same pause has to read as interest rather than disapproval. Whether it will, in this class, on this day, is your call.
Breaking the ask-answer-judge pattern is the larger project this pause belongs to.
pages.wider: This is the neglected half of Rowe's wait time research: the same three seconds, moved to after the answer, where she found it prompts elaboration and self-correction.

why: In open discussion, the quickest thinkers set the terms before anyone else has finished forming a view. A short burst of silent writing before any voice is heard gives every pupil a position of their own to speak from.
The card's phrase is the argument: the pen democratises the room before the voice takes over. It also leaves you thirty written answers to glance at, instead of three spoken ones to remember.
example: Before a discussion on whether the experiment's results support the hypothesis, ninety seconds of silent writing. The teacher then opens the discussion by asking a mid-attaining pupil to read what they wrote, not to improvise something new.
pages.try: One discussion question tomorrow: ninety seconds of writing first, and take the first contribution from the page, not the hand.
notice: Who contributes after writing who would not have contributed before.
The difference in quality between read-from-the-page answers and improvised ones.
consider: Keep the writing short and rough. The moment it becomes a task to complete, it stops being thinking time and starts being work to mark.
It pairs naturally with think, pair, share: write alone, test it on a partner, then speak.
pages.wider: This belongs to the same body of work as think, pair, share: structures that give thinking a protected space before public exposure, so discussion draws on the whole room.

why: Whole-class questioning exposes first-draft thinking to public judgement, which is one reason so many students decline to offer any. Lyman's think-pair-share changes the sequence: thinking time alone, then a pair to test the idea on, then the room.
By the time an idea is spoken publicly it has been formed and rehearsed once already. The card's claim is modest and observable: discussion becomes more considered and more substantive.
example: Asked to predict what happens to the current when a second bulb is added, pupils think alone for thirty seconds, then compare predictions with a partner, then pairs report what they agreed and where they split. The teacher hears reasons, because the pairs have already had to give each other reasons.
pages.try: Take one question you would normally throw open tomorrow and run it as think, pair, share, with the stages timed and kept short.
notice: Contributions from pupils who rarely speak in open discussion.
Whether reported answers refer back to the pair talk: we thought, but then.
What happens in the think stage. If pairs start talking immediately, the individual thinking is being skipped.
consider: The think stage is the one that needs protecting; the structure's value starts with thinking done alone.
Writing during the think stage makes it visible and harder to skip; write before you speak is the natural partner.
pages.wider: Lyman's original structure has barely needed refining: protected thinking, a low-stakes rehearsal, then the room.

why: Hand-raising looks like participation, but Wiliam's point is that it distorts it: a small group volunteers repeatedly and the rest learn that waiting quietly works. The pupils you most need to hear from are usually not the ones with their hands up.
Removing hands and directing questions to named pupils changes the contract. Every pupil now owns the possibility of being asked, which changes how they listen.
example: A teacher tells the class the new normal: hands down unless I ask for them, and I will be choosing. Questions go to named pupils across the fortnight, tracked loosely on a class list so nobody stays invisible. The volunteers grumble for a week; the room's attention changes within days.
pages.try: One class, one week, hands down. Pair it with a visible norm that a wrong attempt is thinking, not failure, or the quiet pupils will experience it as exposure rather than inclusion.
notice: The listening. When anyone might be asked, the question belongs to everyone.
Your own selection pattern. Tracking who you ask, even roughly, tends to reveal habits you did not know you had.
consider: Climate first. The card on cold calling without threat is the necessary companion; direct questioning is only equitable when the room is safe for wrong answers.
Hands still have a place for genuine volunteering, questions to you, and contributions you have not asked for. The change is who controls the distribution of answering.
pages.wider: Good and Brophy's classroom studies documented how questioning patterns quietly reinforce attainment gaps, which is the problem this routine exists to interrupt.

why: Good and Brophy showed that questioning is rarely distributed evenly: teachers direct more questions, and harder ones, to the students they expect more from, and the gap reinforces itself. Cold calling answers that problem only if the climate supports it.
Direct questions are equitable only when a wrong answer costs nothing. The norm the card names carries the whole strategy: no wrong attempts, only thinking.
example: A named pupil offers an answer that is wrong. The teacher treats it as thinking to work with, asks what led them there, and later in the lesson comes back to the same pupil with a related question. The second ask is the message: being wrong did not remove you from the conversation.
pages.try: Establish the norm before you lean on it: name it with the class, and hold the room to it the first time a wrong answer draws a reaction.
notice: What actually happens after a wrong answer: your response, and the room's.
The body language of quieter pupils when names are used. Relief and dread look different.
Whether your harder questions still drift towards the same few students.
consider: Climate is the precondition, not an optional extra. If cold calling in this class would feel like exposure, the norms come first, and how fast to move with a particular anxious pupil is a call for the teacher who knows the class, not a website.
Hands down is the companion routine; this card supplies the conditions that make it fair.
pages.wider: Good and Brophy's work on teacher expectations is the evidence base here; Wiliam's case for questioning every student rests on the same distortion it documents.

why: Almost no teacher believes they distribute questions unevenly until they see their own record. Good and Brophy found harder questions drifting to higher-attaining students, below the level of anyone's awareness, which is why the remedy is a record: patterns invisible in the moment become visible on paper.
You cannot adjust a habit you cannot see, and memory will not supply this picture. A week of tally marks will.
example: A teacher prints the seating plan and keeps a rough tally for a week: a mark for each question asked, a second mark when the question was a demanding one. By Friday the plan shows two desks that were never asked anything, and the demanding marks clustered on one side of the room.
pages.try: One class, one week, tally marks on a printed class list or seating plan. Rough is fine; rough data you collect beats precise data you never do.
notice: Who was never asked at all.
Where the harder questions land, and whether the pattern follows attainment, as Good and Brophy found.
The gap between what you predicted the tally would show and what it shows.
consider: Hands down and cold calling change who you ask; tracking is how you find out whether they are actually working. The three cards make one system.
What to do about a pattern once you can see it is a judgement about individual pupils, and it is yours.
pages.wider: Good and Brophy's expectation studies showed differential questioning operating below teachers' awareness, which is exactly why the remedy is a record rather than a resolution.

why: Wiliam's pose, pause, pounce, bounce packages several of this strand's strategies into one questioning routine: pose the question to everyone, hold the silence, direct it to a named student, then bounce the answer to a second student to extend or challenge.

The bounce is the distinctive move. Because an answer may arrive at anyone, everyone has a reason to listen to it; the card describes it as keeping all students alert and spreading thinking across the whole room.
example: What was the turning point in this experiment? Pause, while everyone thinks. Then: Jacob? Jacob answers. The teacher does not evaluate, but bounces it: Priya, would you add anything to Jacob's reason, or push back on it? The judgement that would normally come from the front comes instead from the room.
pages.try: Script one question through all four steps for tomorrow, including who you might pounce to and who you might bounce to. Improvising the routine comes later; start deliberate.
notice: Listening during and after the first answer, now that it might land on anyone.
The quality of the bounced response compared with the first answer.
Whether you are pausing for long enough. Without the pause, the pounce becomes a speed test.
consider: Bouncing a wrong answer to another student needs the no-threat climate to be real first, or the first student pays for the routine.
The pause is wait time 1 doing its usual work; the routine inherits everything Rowe found about it.
pages.wider: The routine is Wiliam's, from the same body of formative assessment work as hands down; Rowe's wait time research explains why the pause is not optional.

why: Alexander names five qualities of dialogic talk: collective, reciprocal, supportive, cumulative and purposeful. The list works as a diagnostic, because most classroom talk already meets two or three of the five.

That is what makes this card practical rather than aspirational. You are not building dialogic talk from nothing; you are finding the missing qualities and working on those. Audit, and start with the gaps.
example: A teacher asks a colleague to observe a discussion lesson with just the five words on a slip of paper. The verdict: collective and supportive, clearly; reciprocal, sometimes; cumulative, rarely. Contributions sat side by side without building on each other. That one word, cumulative, becomes the focus for the term.
pages.try: Audit one discussion this week against the five qualities, honestly. Two or three ticks is the expected result, not a failure.
notice: Which of the five are reliably present in your classroom talk, and which never appear.
Whether contributions chain, each building on the last, or simply accumulate.
Whether the talk is going somewhere planned, which is what purposeful asks.
consider: Start with the gaps rather than everything at once; the card is explicit on this.
Several other cards in this cluster target one quality each: ground rules build the collective and supportive, building on responses builds the cumulative. The audit tells you which to reach for.
pages.wider: Alexander's dialogic teaching is the broadest framework in this strand, and the five principles are its most practical point of entry.

why: Ask, answer, judge. The IRE pattern, initiation, response, evaluation, is the default grammar of classroom talk, and Alexander shows it limits thinking: every exchange is three moves long and ends with a verdict from the front.
The fix on the card is small enough to try today. Replace the evaluation with a follow-up question: what makes you say that? The exchange stays open, and the reasoning has to come out.
example: A pupil answers that the metal expands when heated. Instead of good, the teacher asks what makes you say that. The pupil explains, and the explanation shows what they think the particles are doing, which turns out to be the thing worth teaching next.
pages.try: Pick one lesson and replace every evaluative response with either a follow-up question or three seconds of nothing.
notice: How often you evaluate. The pattern is nearly impossible to hear from inside, which is why the card points at capturing a lesson to listen back to.
How long exchanges become when the third move is a question rather than a verdict.
Whether pupils start justifying answers before being asked to.
consider: What makes you say that works on right answers too. Probing only the wrong ones teaches the class to read your follow-ups as a signal.
Wait time 2 breaks the same pattern with silence rather than a question; some exchanges want one, some the other.

Capturing a lesson to listen back to means recording people, and that requires consent. Whether and how you record is down to your school or trust policy: seek that answer before you press record, not after.
pages.wider: Alexander and Mercer both treat IRE as the pattern to escape from; most of the dialogic cluster is, one way or another, an alternative third move.

why: Mercer distinguishes three kinds of group talk. Disputational: I am right, you are wrong. Cumulative: agreement piled on agreement, nothing examined. Exploratory: ideas challenged with evidence and built on together. Only the third improves outcomes.

Exploratory talk is what this strand's thinking describes: pupils reasoning together and making their thinking public. It seldom appears on its own, which is why the ground rules card follows this one.
example: A group is deciding where to site a settlement. One pupil proposes the valley floor for the water supply; another challenges with the flood risk shown on the map; the proposal gets reworked to the terrace above. Challenge carrying evidence, then building: that is the shape to listen for.
pages.try: Listen in on one group task this week and ask which of the three kinds of talk you are hearing. Naming it is the diagnostic step.
notice: Whether disagreement comes with evidence or just with volume.
Whether any idea actually changes during the talk. In cumulative talk, nothing does.
Who inside a group is doing the reasoning, and who is assenting.
consider: Disputational and cumulative talk are not misbehaviour; they are what groups default to before the norms of exploratory talk are taught. The ground rules card is the companion piece.
tech: A collaborative document or discussion tool from your school's approved set can hold a group's reasoning as it develops and keep it afterwards, so a useful discussion does not disappear the moment the lesson moves on. The test stays the same: the tool should widen who contributes to the reasoning, never do the reasoning for them.
pages.wider: Mercer's studies of group talk are the source, and they connect directly to his work on interthinking: exploratory talk is how thinking becomes genuinely shared.

why: Groups do not fall into exploratory talk by accident. Mercer found that teaching its norms transforms discussion, with one detail that changes how you should do it: norms co-constructed with the class outperform norms displayed or modelled.
The making is part of the mechanism. Rules a class wrote together are rules they can hold each other to.
example: A class spends ten minutes drafting its own rules for discussion: everyone's ideas get considered, reasons are asked for, we try to agree before we move on. The wording is the pupils' own. It goes on the wall afterwards because they wrote it, not so that they will read it.
pages.try: Before the next discussion-heavy topic, give ten minutes to agreeing the ground rules with the class instead of presenting yours.
notice: Whether pupils invoke the rules unprompted during group work.
Who enforces them when they are broken: you, or the group.
consider: Co-construction is the active ingredient. The card is explicit that displayed or modelled norms underperform, so resisting the efficient shortcut is the strategy.
Success criteria built with the class work by a similar mechanism, which is why the formative assessment strand has a sibling card.
pages.wider: This comes from the same programme of Mercer's research as exploratory talk; the ground rules are how that kind of talk is taught rather than hoped for.

why: Michaels, O'Connor and Resnick's accountable talk holds discussion to two standards at once: accurate knowledge and rigorous reasoning. The route in is language. Teach the moves explicitly: I agree because, the evidence is, say more.
The card's last three words carry the theory: language shapes thinking. Give pupils the sentence shapes of reasoning and you give the reasoning somewhere to go.
example: During a discussion of a historical source, the sentence starters sit on the board. A pupil begins, the evidence is, and then has to find some in the source before the sentence can end. The stem does not decorate the claim; it obliges the pupil to complete it.
pages.try: Introduce two of the moves, not the whole set, and ask for them in one discussion this week.
notice: Whether the stems are changing the reasoning or just the phrasing around it.
Which moves pupils adopt without prompting, and whether say more starts passing between pupils rather than only from you.
consider: Accountability here is to knowledge and reasoning, not to talking more; a short contribution with evidence beats a long one without.
The stems are scaffolds, and scaffolds are for fading once the habits of reasoning stand on their own.
pages.wider: Accountable talk comes from Michaels, O'Connor and Resnick's long programme of work on academically productive talk, and it shares its ground with Mercer: the quality of talk is teachable.

why: When Alexander's dialogic teaching approach was trialled with the EEF, one teacher move stood out: extending student responses rather than evaluating them. The card's image is exact: conductor, not judge.

Returning an answer to the room, Aisha says X, does anyone want to add or challenge, does two things at once. It relieves you of the verdict, and it makes the class the audience for each other's thinking rather than spectators to yours.
example: Discussing a poem's ending, a pupil says it feels hopeful. The teacher returns it: Sam thinks the ending is hopeful. Who wants to add to that, or push against it? Three more contributions arrive before the teacher speaks again, and the third disagrees with the first, politely, with a line from the poem.
pages.try: Choose one returning phrase, does anyone want to add or challenge that, and use it in place of your usual evaluation for a single lesson.
notice: How long chains of pupil contributions run before you re-enter.
Whether pupils begin addressing each other by name rather than routing everything through you.
What your withheld verdict does to the pupil who answered; the pause after their answer is wait time 2 in action.
consider: Conducting is still steering. You choose whose answer gets returned and when to close a line down; extending is not abdicating.
Returning a wrong answer for the class to work on needs the same climate as cold calling, or the pupil hears it as public marking.
pages.wider: Alexander's EEF-trialled dialogic teaching programme is the direct source; extending rather than evaluating was one of its core teacher moves.

why: King's finding reverses the usual direction of classroom questioning: students trained to generate questions from stems produce richer discussion than students answering only the teacher's questions. Generating a question demands deeper processing than answering one.
The stems do the lifting. Without them, student questions tend towards what is X; with them, pupils reach for connections and consequences they would not have phrased alone.
example: At the end of an explanation in science, three stems go on the board: how does ... affect ...? what would happen if ...? how does ... connect to what we learned about ...? Every pupil writes one question about the topic, and a handful get posed back to the class.
pages.try: Display two or three stems after your next explanation and have every pupil write one question before any discussion starts.
notice: The level of the questions against the stems' demand: are pupils using the stems, or writing what is X underneath them?
Questions that reveal gaps or misconceptions; a generated question is evidence as well as enquiry.
How discussion of a pupil's question differs from discussion of yours.
consider: Stems need modelling like anything else; write a few questions with the class before expecting them alone.
The generation is where the processing happens, so the questions are worth something even when there is no time to answer them all.
pages.wider: King's guided questioning studies sit behind this whole cluster; the stems are her mechanism for lifting student questions above recall.

why: King's reciprocal questioning takes question stems one step further: students generate questions and pose them to each other, with neither the asker nor the answerer knowing the answer in advance. That last condition is the interesting one. It produces genuine enquiry rather than rehearsal.
The card's closing instruction is the spirit of the thing: aim to think.
example: After a fortnight's work on the circulatory system, pairs each write a question using the stems, swap, and work on answers together. One pair lands on a question about why valves fail that neither can answer, and brings it to the teacher; the question becomes the next lesson's opening.
pages.try: Run it first on content already taught, with stems provided and ten minutes protected: one question each, swap, then talk through the answers together.
notice: Whether pairs are enquiring or rehearsing: questions they already know the answers to are practice, not this.
The talk while answering. At its best it sounds like exploratory talk in miniature.
The questions neither pupil can answer, which are information for you.
consider: Teaching the stems comes first; this card assumes the previous one.
When a pair is stuck, the temptation to hand over the answer is strong. A good question is meant to be wrestled with; give the struggle a little room before you shorten it.
pages.wider: King tested reciprocal peer questioning directly against discussion of teacher questions; the distinction between enquiry and rehearsal is hers.

why: A student's question reveals the depth of their understanding, often more precisely than their answer to yours. Why does X cause Y? comes from somewhere different than what is X?, and the difference is diagnostic. Questions are windows.
The routine on the card is deliberately small: one written question from each student before they leave.
example: At the end of a lesson on photosynthesis, every pupil writes one question. They range from what is chlorophyll again to why do plants need glucose if they are making oxygen. Read together, the pile locates the class: who is still at naming, who is connecting, and which misconception has survived the lesson.
notice: The level of the questions, what against why, and how it shifts across a topic.
Pupils whose questions sit far above or below what their written work suggested.
Which questions repeat across the class; a question many pupils ask is a teaching point, not a coincidence.
consider: The questions are only evidence if they change something. Reading them into the next lesson's plan is the other half of the routine.
Question stems raise the quality of what pupils can ask; the two cards work together.
tech: An approved exit ticket or response tool will gather a question from every pupil in the closing minutes, including those who would never ask one aloud, and it keeps the set in one place to read while planning what comes next. The tool manages the collecting; the reading, and deciding what to do about it, stays with you.
pages.wider: King's research explains why generating a question is so revealing; Wiliam's explains what to do with the evidence once you have it.

why: Interthinking is Mercer's word for something classrooms can be unusually good at: cognition genuinely shared, built between people through language. Student questions are what keep that joint enquiry moving.
The card's distinction is the one to hold onto: the goal is thinking in common, not performance for the teacher.
