example: A group is working out why their bridge design failed under load. The questions that move the work along pass between pupils: was it the joints or the span? how do we test that without breaking the second one? Nothing routes through the teacher, and the enquiry belongs to the group.
pages.try: Sit near one group during a task and count how many of the questions asked are pupil-to-pupil rather than pupil-to-you.
notice: Whether questions route through you or across the group.
Whether a pupil's question ever changes the group's direction; that is joint enquiry doing its work.
How the talk changes when you approach. A group performing for the teacher sounds different from a group thinking.
consider: Exploratory talk is the ground this grows in; groups that have not learned its norms will find it hard to interthink, whatever the task.
pages.wider: Interthinking is where Mercer's work on classroom talk arrives: language not just expressing thought but doing the thinking, jointly.

why: The know and want-to-know routine is familiar enough to feel like habit. King's research gives it a firmer footing: questions connected to prior knowledge produce the most powerful learning, and asking students to write what they know and what they want to know surfaces both halves at once.
Their questions become the entry point into the content, rather than an opening activity to be filed away.
example: Opening a unit on space, pupils write two short lists: what they already know, and what they want to know. The teacher reads both before planning the next lesson. The first list shows the prior knowledge to connect to, and one misconception to unpick; the second supplies three questions good enough to teach through.
pages.try: Ten minutes at the start of your next new topic: know and want to know, written and collected in, not just discussed.
notice: Prior knowledge you did not expect, in both directions.
Which pupil questions could anchor a whole lesson, and which reveal what the class thinks the topic is about.
Whether pupils notice their own questions being answered as the unit unfolds.
consider: Entry point, not itinerary. The scheme of work still sets the destination, and what to do with the questions it cannot accommodate is your call.
Collecting the lists in writing keeps every pupil's starting point visible, not just the confident talkers'.
pages.wider: King's finding about prior knowledge connects this card to a principle that runs through the whole guide: new learning holds best when it is fastened to what is already there.

why: New material arrives faster than it can be processed. Rosenshine's first principle is blunt about the remedy: present new material in small steps, with practice after each one, because working memory is narrow and easily overwhelmed.
The discipline sits in the practice-after-each part. A step without a check is just a pause, and telling is not explaining.
example: Introducing balancing equations, a science teacher builds the method one move per slide, using animation to reveal each step. After each reveal, pupils try one line of a parallel problem on mini whiteboards before the next step appears.
pages.try: Take one explanation you already have planned and mark where each genuinely new idea begins. Those marks are your steps; add a short piece of practice after each one.
notice: Where the wheels come off. With small steps, confusion surfaces at a specific step rather than at the end of a long explanation.
Whether the practice after each step is completed by everyone, or only by those who were already keeping up.
consider: Step size is a judgement about this class and their prior knowledge; what is one step for a second teaching may be three for a first. The teacher knows the class, not a website.
Small steps are not slow teaching; checking as you go can save the longer reteach later.
pages.wider: Rosenshine's principles of instruction distilled decades of research on effective teaching into this sequence, and Sweller's cognitive load theory explains why it works.

why: Abstract ideas are hard to hold when there is nothing to attach them to. Willingham's advice is to anchor new ideas to concrete examples first: make the thing visible, then name it.
Naming first inverts the load. Pupils are asked to store a definition while still hunting for what it refers to.
example: Before the word erosion appears anywhere, a geography teacher plays a short clip of a riverbank collapsing, then shows photographs of the same stretch a year apart. Only once the class has described what they can see does the term arrive to label it.
pages.try: For one abstract term in next week's teaching, find the image, clip or object first, and plan to show it before you say the word.
notice: Whether pupils reach for the concrete example when they explain the idea back to you.
What happens when the abstract term is tested later: does the anchor come back with it?
consider: The concrete is a bridge, not a destination. The card is explicit: move to the abstract once the concrete is secure, and judging secure is a call only the teacher in the room can make.
pages.wider: Willingham's cognitive science writing for teachers is the source here: understanding is built out of things already understood, which is why the concrete example comes first.

why: Nothing you explain lands on a blank slate. Rosenshine's advice is to connect to prior knowledge before introducing anything new, because the new idea has to attach to something already there.
Link before you launch, as the card puts it. The few minutes spent activating what pupils already know may decide how much of the explanation sticks.
example: Before starting a unit on the causes of the First World War, a history teacher puts a concept map on screen and asks the class to retrieve what they remember about empire and alliances from the previous term. The gaps that show up shape how the new explanation begins.
pages.try: Open your next new topic with a two-minute retrieval starter on the specific ideas the explanation depends on, not general revision.
notice: What the starter reveals. If the prior knowledge is not there, the explanation you planned needs adjusting before it starts.
Whether pupils use the retrieved ideas of their own accord during the new material.
consider: The starter is diagnostic, not decorative; be ready to act on what it shows, even if that means reteaching before launching.
Choose retrieval targets that genuinely underpin the new content. Activating unrelated knowledge fills working memory without helping the explanation.
pages.wider: This is one of Rosenshine's principles of instruction, part of the same distilled research base that gives the strand its small-steps sequence.

why: It is easy to assume the more sophisticated tool teaches better. The EEF found otherwise: clarity matters more than delivery method, and a diagram under a visualiser can outperform a polished video.
So the question to ask of any display is not whether it is impressive but whether it makes this idea clearest for this class.
example: Planning to teach the structure of the heart, a science teacher weighs a slick animation against drawing and labelling the diagram live under a visualiser, and chooses the live drawing: the class sees the structure assembled one part at a time, at the pace of the explanation.
notice: Whether pupils can restate the idea afterwards, whichever display you chose.
Whether time spent producing a resource is reflected in what the class understood. Effort and clarity are not the same thing.
consider: Clearest is a judgement about a particular idea and a particular class, and only the teacher in the room can make it.
There is nothing wrong with a new tool as such; the test is whether it makes the idea clearer than what you already do.
pages.wider: The EEF's review of digital technology in classrooms sits behind this card; its finding that clarity beats delivery method is the whole strategy.

why: A class that listens politely looks identical to a class that understands. Listening is not learning, and an explanation that is never checked is a guess about thirty minds.
Rosenshine's answer is to check understanding at every step and reteach before moving on. The explanation is the start, not the finish.
example: Halfway through explaining photosynthesis, a teacher poses one question to the whole class and every pupil answers on a mini whiteboard. The spread of answers decides what happens next: move on, or reteach the step that wobbled.
pages.try: Plan one check into the middle of your next explanation, answered by everyone at once rather than by one volunteer.
notice: The gap between who looked like they were following and who showed they were.
What the wrong answers have in common. A shared error usually points at the explanation, not the pupils.
How often the check changes what you do next. If it never does, it has become a ritual rather than a check.
consider: Checking every step changes your pacing, and that is the point rather than a cost; Rosenshine's sequence assumes you will sometimes reteach.
Whole-class response beats sampling one or two hands, because the pupils you do not hear from are the ones assumptions get made about.
pages.wider: Checks for understanding are central to Rosenshine's principles of instruction; this card is that principle applied to the middle of an explanation rather than the end.

why: Once an explanation is recorded, it is tempting to let the recording do the teaching. The EEF's finding pushes the other way: technology works best when it supplements teaching, not when it replaces it.
A screencast cannot see puzzled faces, take a question or reteach a step. It works alongside your classroom explanation, not instead of it.
example: After teaching a method live, a maths teacher posts a short screencast of the same method to the class page. Pupils who were absent, or who want it again before the homework, replay it; the live lesson is unchanged.
pages.try: Before recording anything, name what the recording adds that the live explanation cannot: replay, pause, access after absence. If you cannot name one, skip the recording.
notice: Who uses the replays, and when. Use clustered before homework or assessment tells you something different from no use at all.
Whether the questions asked in lessons change once replays exist.
consider: The live explanation stays primary. If the screencast starts standing in for teaching rather than backing it up, the balance has tipped.
tech: A screencast made with the approved screen recording tool in your setting, shared through your school's learning platform, gives an explanation a second life: pupils can pause, rewind and revisit. That is the supplement. The moment it becomes the first and only telling, it is a substitute, and that is not where the EEF's evidence says technology works best.
pages.wider: The EEF's digital technology guidance is the direct source; supplement, never substitute is its finding compressed into four words.

why: Working memory holds about four items, and every element on your screen bids for one of those slots. A logo, a border, a sentence nobody needs right now: each one is renting space the explanation requires.
Sweller's point is structural, not stylistic. Stripping slides to essentials is load management, and so is pressing B to blank the screen when you want attention on you.
example: A teacher preparing to explain supply and demand cuts the slide to one graph and a four-word heading. When the discussion moves beyond the graph, the B key blanks the screen and the class's four slots go to the speaking voice.
pages.try: Count the elements on each slide of the deck you will teach next. Anything beyond the essentials is a candidate for deletion, and the B key covers the moments when the essential thing is you.
notice: Where pupils look during the explanation, with a full screen and with a blank one.
Whether recall improves on the ideas taught from stripped slides. If nothing changes, look at what else is loading the moment.
consider: What counts as essential depends on the idea and the class; the four-item limit is general, but the editing is local.
A blank screen shifts the whole load onto your spoken explanation, which is why this pairs with small steps.
pages.wider: Sweller's cognitive load theory supplies the mechanism: working memory is narrow and easily overwhelmed, and explanation is an act of load management.

why: Put the labels in one place and the diagram in another and pupils must search between them, holding fragments in mind while their eyes travel. Sweller calls this split attention, and the searching spends exactly the working memory the explanation needs.
Integrating labels directly into the image removes the search. Nothing about the content changes; only the cost of reading it.
example: Teaching the water cycle, a teacher shows the diagram unlabelled and adds each label live with an annotation tool, placing the word on the part it names while explaining that stage. The class never has to match a numbered key to the picture.
pages.try: Find one resource you use where the key or captions sit apart from the image, and move the words onto the image itself.
notice: Whether the which-bit-is-that questions disappear.
How pupils label their own diagrams afterwards, and whether the integrated layout gets copied.
consider: Building the labels live does two jobs at once: it integrates the information and it paces the reveal to your explanation.
When you cannot edit a printed resource, annotating it under a visualiser achieves the same integration.
pages.wider: Split attention comes from Sweller's cognitive load research; Mayer's spatial contiguity principle is the same insight arrived at through multimedia learning.

why: Reading text aloud while the same text sits on the screen feels thorough. Sweller's redundancy effect says it is the opposite: pupils process the written and spoken versions at once, the two streams compete, and working memory pays for both.
The fix costs nothing. Say it, or show it, and stop doing both at the same time. Explaining is an act of load management, and this is the single easiest load to remove.
example: Mid-explanation, a teacher presses B. The screen goes black, thirty pairs of eyes come up, and the idea gets explained in speech with nothing competing for attention. When the diagram is needed, the screen comes back, and the teacher talks over the image rather than reading beside it.
pages.try: Take one slide you will teach this week, delete the sentences and keep the image. Say the deleted words instead. The B key, or W for a white screen, does the same job mid-flow.
notice: Where pupils look when the screen is blank against when it is full of text.
What the checks for understanding say afterwards. Cleaner explanation should show up as cleaner recall, and if it does not, that is worth knowing too.
consider: The effect is about simultaneous duplication. Text pupils need to read silently, in their own time, is a different situation and a legitimate one.
A blank screen puts the weight on your spoken explanation, which is exactly why this pairs with small steps and the other load principles in the strand.
pages.wider: Sweller's cognitive load theory explains the mechanism, and Mayer's multimedia principles map when words and images combine well and when they collide; the strand's further reading covers both.

why: Busy slides feel rich and teach little. Mayer's coherence principle is uncompromising: remove every word, image and sound that does not support the learning, because each one competes for attention precisely when the explanation needs space.
Clip art, background music, a themed border: none of it is neutral. If it is on the screen, it is being processed.
example: Rebuilding a slide sequence on the digestive system, a teacher deletes the cartoon stomach, the sound effects and two of the three photographs, leaving one clear diagram and a handful of words. The content taught is identical; the competition for attention is not.
pages.try: Open tomorrow's deck and remove everything decorative from a single slide. Teach it, and notice whether anything is actually missed.
notice: Where attention settles once the decoration is gone.
Whether recall centres on the idea or on whatever accompanied it.
consider: The hardest cuts are the interesting ones. The test is not whether an element is engaging but whether it supports the learning; the coherence principle draws the line there.
Decoration for one class may be scaffold for another; what supports learning is judged in the room, not in the template.
pages.wider: Mayer's coherence principle, part of his cognitive theory of multimedia learning, is the source; Sweller's load theory explains what the clutter costs.

why: Show a class a dense diagram or a long passage and every pupil must work out alone where to look. Mayer's signalling principle offers the fix: bold, arrows and highlights direct attention to the part the explanation is about.
Without a signal, learners search alone, and some will still be searching when the explanation moves on.
example: Analysing a poem on screen, an English teacher highlights the two words under discussion as they are discussed, live, with an annotation tool. The whole class reads the same poem, but everyone is looking at the same two words at the same moment.
pages.try: Next time a text or diagram is on screen, annotate it live during the explanation instead of presenting it pre-marked.
notice: How quickly eyes find the feature you are discussing.
Whether pupils' own notes and annotations pick out the features you signalled, or different ones.
consider: Signal sparingly. A slide where everything is bold has no signal at all.
Live annotation ties the signal to your voice, so attention and narration move together.
pages.wider: Signalling is one of Mayer's multimedia principles, developed from the same research programme as coherence and segmenting.

why: Delivered as one continuous stream, an explanation gives working memory nowhere to catch up. Mayer's segmenting principle breaks the content into chunks, with processing time between them.
On screen, that means one idea per click. The pause after each chunk is where the processing happens.
example: A teacher explaining the stages of mitosis sets the diagram to build across five clicks. Between clicks, a question or a ten-second look at the board gives each chunk time to settle before the next arrives.
pages.try: Take one slide that currently shows everything at once and rebuild it so each idea appears on its own click.
notice: Whether the pauses that feel long to you land differently with the class.
The questions that come between chunks, which can surface confusion while the idea is still small.
consider: Click, not auto-play. The card is specific because the difference is who controls the pace: you, reading the room, or the software, reading a timer.
pages.wider: Mayer's segmenting principle is the direct source, and it is the multimedia expression of the same limit Sweller's load theory describes.

why: Words and images reach the mind through separate channels, and Paivio's dual coding theory says using both gives the same idea two routes in.
The design instruction that follows: pair a key visual with minimal text, both carrying the one idea.
example: For a lesson on trench warfare, the slide holds one cross-section image and six words of labelling. The teacher's narration does the explaining; the image and the sparse text give the idea its second route.
pages.try: Choose one text-only slide and find the visual that shows its idea. Cut the text to the few words the visual cannot carry.
notice: Whether pupils sketch when they try to recall the idea, and what their sketches keep.
Whether the image comes back when the words are tested later.
consider: Two routes to the same idea, not two ideas at once. An unrelated image is clutter, not coding.
Minimal text is part of the theory, not a style preference; the redundancy and coherence cards explain what fuller text costs.
pages.wider: Paivio laid out dual coding theory, and Mayer built on it in the cognitive theory of multimedia learning; this card is the theory applied to a single slide.

why: An image explained by on-screen text asks the eyes to do two jobs at once. Mayer's modality principle found people learn better from images with narration than from images with text, because the voice takes one channel and the image the other.
Let the voice do what text would overload, as the card has it. The strand prose makes the same call: narrate a diagram rather than captioning it.
example: Recording an explanation of longshore drift, a teacher screencasts the diagram and speaks the explanation over it, the cursor tracing the movement being described. No paragraphs on screen; the words arrive by ear while the eyes follow the coast.
pages.try: Take one diagram you usually present with written explanation beside it, strip the text back to bare labels, and speak the explanation instead, live or recorded.
notice: Where pupils look while you narrate, compared with when there was text to read.
On a recorded version, where pupils pause and replay; those points can map the difficult moments.
consider: Modality moves the explanatory prose to the voice; short labels that simply name parts still belong on the image, which is what the contiguity card covers.
pages.wider: Mayer's modality principle is the source, resting on the dual channel model that Paivio's work established.

why: Each stretch of screen between a label and the thing it names has to be crossed by the eye and bridged by memory. Mayer's spatial contiguity principle keeps words next to the images they describe, so nothing needs holding during the journey.
A numbered key below a diagram is the classic offender: accurate, complete, and in the wrong place.
example: Laying out a slide on the parts of a flower, a teacher places each label beside its structure with a short connecting line, rather than listing the names in a panel down the side. Reading the slide and reading the diagram become the same act.
pages.try: Scan the resources for your next topic for separated captions, keys and label lists, and move each word next to the thing it names.
notice: How long it takes pupils to find a named part on the diagram.
Whether questions about the diagram use the labels' vocabulary.
consider: The principle applies wherever words and images share a surface: worksheets, wall displays and textbook pages, not just slides.
For a resource you cannot redesign, annotating it live under a visualiser puts the words where they belong.
pages.wider: Spatial contiguity is one of Mayer's multimedia principles and shares its mechanism with Sweller's split attention effect.

why: A finished slide shows everything at once, but an explanation happens over time. Progressive reveal closes that gap, adding content one step at a time so the display keeps pace with the telling.
Anything visible before you reach it risks being read instead of listened to.
example: Building an annotated map of a battle across eight clicks, a teacher adds each movement as it enters the story. At any moment the screen shows exactly as much as has been explained, no more.
pages.try: Set every element of your next full slide to appear on click, then teach it and click only when the explanation arrives at each element.
notice: Whether reading ahead stops.
Which reveals you hold back longest when teaching live; those are the steps your explanation needs most time on.
consider: The reveal serves the narration, not the spectacle. A plain appear does the job; movement for its own sake is clutter in motion.
One idea per click keeps you honest about how much each step contains, which is small steps by another route.
pages.wider: The card draws on both Mayer's segmenting principle and Sweller's account of working memory: pacing the display is pacing the load.

why: A long recorded explanation is easy to make and hard to use. Mayer's evidence points at images plus voice outperforming text-heavy slides, and the card adds the discipline: one idea per video, because brevity beats completeness.
Completeness is what the whole library is for. Each clip only has to do one job.
example: A maths teacher records one screencast on expanding a single bracket: the working shown on screen, the voice narrating over it, nothing else. The next idea, a second bracket, gets its own separate recording.
pages.try: Record one short screencast this week on the single idea you are asked to repeat most often.
notice: Which clips get replayed, and where pupils pause them.
Whether the repeat explanations that prompted the recording actually reduce.
consider: One idea per video is the whole discipline; when a recording starts needing chapters, it is several videos.
These are supplements to your live explanation, not a substitute for it; the strand is firm on that distinction.

How short is short is your call to make; the reason to keep making it is working memory. It's narrow, and every extra idea in a video competes for the space the first one needs. When in doubt, split the recording.
tech: The approved screen recording tool in your setting is all this needs: record the screen, narrate over it, share through your usual platform. Keep the design rules from the rest of the strand inside the recording too: minimal text, one clear visual, the voice doing the explaining.
pages.wider: Mayer's multimedia research underpins both halves of the card: the choice of narrated visuals and the case for keeping each segment small.

why: An explanation delivered in unfamiliar terms is two lessons compressed into one, and working memory pays for both at once. Mayer's pre-training principle separates them: teach the key terms first, then the ideas.
Learners who already know the words can give the explanation their full attention, as the card puts it: they can focus on the ideas.
example: Before a lesson on electrical circuits, pupils meet current, voltage and resistance on a vocabulary slide, or in a short pre-lesson video, with a picture for each. When the main explanation uses the terms, they label something half-known rather than arriving as new noise.
pages.try: List the terms your next explanation cannot be given without, and teach the unfamiliar ones before it starts rather than pausing to define them mid-flow.
notice: Whether questions during the explanation are about the words or about the ideas.
Whether the pre-trained terms show up in pupils' own talk and writing.
consider: How many terms need pre-training, and which, is a judgement about this class; the teacher knows who is meeting each word for the first time.
Pre-training pairs naturally with connecting to prior knowledge: one prepares the words, the other the ideas they will attach to.

stair.lede: Drafting a tight vocabulary list with pupil-friendly definitions is a job AI handles well, through the approved tool in your setting:
stair.prompt:
Act as a secondary science teacher. From the topic outline below, identify the six terms Year 8 pupils must know before an explanation of the topic, and write a one-sentence pupil-friendly definition for each.

Keep definitions concrete and free of other technical terms. Present as a plain list, term then definition, nothing else.

[paste your topic outline here]
stair.after: You know which terms your class already holds; cut and swap until the list is genuinely the six that unlock the explanation. Iteration is essential, and the definitions must match how you'll use the terms in the room.

pages.wider: Pre-training is one of Mayer's multimedia principles, and its logic is pure cognitive load theory: reduce what is novel at the moment of explanation.
tech: A vocabulary slide or a short pre-lesson video, made with the approved tools in your setting, puts the terms in front of pupils before the explanation needs them.

why: Experts make invisible decisions constantly: where to start, what to check, when something looks wrong. Pupils see the finished product and none of the decisions, then are asked to produce the same kind of product themselves.
Thinking aloud while you work makes the invisible expertise visible. It is modelling the process rather than the product, and the process is what novices actually need to copy.
example: Under a visualiser, a teacher annotates an unseen source, narrating the decisions: I am reading the provenance line first, because it changes how I weigh everything else. I am not sure about this phrase yet, so I am marking it and moving on. The narration is the lesson; the finished annotation is just its residue.
pages.try: Choose one task this week that you would normally demonstrate silently or show finished, and narrate your way through it live: the choices, the checks, and what you do when unsure.
notice: What shows up in pupils' subsequent attempts. Copied structure and copied self-checks are the strategy working; copied surface features are a sign the narration stayed too shallow.
The questions pupils ask afterwards, which tend to move from what is the answer towards how did you know to do that.
consider: Narrating decisions is different from narrating actions. Now I underline the date is a caption; I am underlining the date because it tells me which rules apply is thinking made audible.
This is the start of a handover, not the whole of one. The strand's scaffolding strategies describe the fade from modelled to guided to independent.
pages.wider: Rosenshine's principles put modelling and worked examples at the centre of effective instruction; thinking aloud is those principles applied to the parts of expertise pupils cannot otherwise see.
tech: The visualiser is the stage here, and a screen recording of the same narration gives pupils the modelling on replay, pausable at the exact moment they lost the thread. Use the approved tools in your setting for both. The technology carries the modelling; it doesn't replace it.

why: Modelling only teaches the pupils who can see it. A visualiser turns any desk into a stage: handwriting, annotation, a diagram taking shape, all visible to the whole room at once.
The EEF found the visualiser among the most promising classroom technology, which is striking for such a modest device. It changes nothing about the work and everything about who can watch it happen.
example: Redrafting a paragraph under the camera, an English teacher crosses out, substitutes and rereads in front of the class, the page filling with visible second thoughts. The same demonstration at a desk would have reached the front row.
pages.try: Put one ordinary thing under the visualiser this week: your own working, a source, a pupil's draft shared with permission, and teach from it.
notice: Whether every seat genuinely has a sightline, including the corners.
What changes when the work on the stage is a pupil's rather than yours.
consider: The stage is for process. Rosenshine's advice is to model the working, not display the finished product; a visualiser makes the crossings-out public, and that is its value.
Sharing pupil work under the camera depends on the culture in the room, and the teacher is the judge of when a class is ready for it.
pages.wider: The EEF's technology guidance supplies the evidence of promise, and Rosenshine's principles supply the reason: modelling sits at the centre of effective instruction.

why: Sweller and Cooper showed students can learn more from studying worked examples than from solving equivalent problems, but a worked example on the board lasts only as long as the lesson allows.
Recording it changes the arithmetic. A screencast of the method can be paused, rewound and studied at each pupil's own pace, which suits the way novices need to see a process unfold.
example: Working a full solution to a quadratic on screen, a teacher records the process, narration included, and posts it to the class page. That evening one pupil pauses at the factorising step three times; another skims to the final line to check their own working.
pages.try: Record the worked example you were going to do anyway: point the approved screen recording tool at it while you teach, and share the result.
notice: Where the pauses and rewinds cluster, if your platform shows you.
Whether pupils refer back to the method mid-practice, or only check final answers.
consider: The replay supplements the live modelling; the thinking aloud, the checks and the questions still happen in the room.
Pairing recorded examples with practice problems, example then attempt, is where the next card takes this.
tech: A screen recording made with the approved tool in your setting and shared through your learning platform is the whole setup; the value sits in the replayable method, not in production polish.
pages.wider: Sweller and Cooper's worked example research, a central finding of cognitive load theory, is the direct source.

why: Teach five examples then set ten problems and the method has faded before the first attempt. Atkinson's research supports a tighter weave: alternate worked examples with practice. Example, try. Example, try.
Each attempt comes while the example is still fresh, and each fresh example arrives just after pupils have discovered what they needed it for.
example: On screen: a worked percentage-change example. Then a structurally identical problem for pupils to try. Then a second example with different numbers, then a second attempt. The display alternates between showing and asking for the length of the practice phase.
notice: Error rates on the first attempt after each example, compared with the long-block approach you used before.
Whether pupils look back at the example mid-attempt, and what they look for.
consider: Parallel means genuinely parallel: same structure, different surface. A task that changes the structure is a new example pretending to be practice.
How long to keep alternating before moving to unsupported problems is a fading decision, and that judgement belongs with the teacher who can see the attempts.

stair.lede: The example-try rhythm eats parallel practice questions. Drafting them, matched to your worked example, is a strong use of AI through the approved tool in your setting:
stair.prompt:
Act as a secondary maths teacher. Below is a worked example I will model for Year 9. Create four practice problems that follow exactly the same method and structure, changing only the numbers and surface context.

Order them from most similar to the example to least. Do not include solutions, hints or method notes.

[paste your worked example here]
stair.after: Check each problem really does exercise the same method, not a lookalike that needs a different move; that's the check only a subject teacher can make. Iterate until the set is right, then run example, try, example, try.

pages.wider: Atkinson's work on alternating examples with practice builds directly on Sweller's worked example effect; the two are cited together on the card for good reason.
tech: The pattern needs nothing more than a display for the example and a task alongside it, using the approved tools in your setting.

why: Support that never fades teaches dependence on the support; support removed all at once tips pupils into overload. Rosenshine's resolution is a gradient: a complete example, then a partial one with gaps, then independent practice.
The fading is the teaching. Each removed piece hands one more part of the thinking to the pupil, at a rate working memory can absorb.
example: A fillable template structures a science evaluation three times over: first fully modelled, then with the reasoning sentences gapped, then blank. The same document, hollowed out in stages, walks the class from watching to doing.
pages.try: Take one task you currently model in full and build the middle version: the same example with strategic gaps for pupils to complete.
notice: Which gaps get filled confidently and which stall a row of pens; the stalls show where the thinking actually lives.
Who still reaches for the complete version, and for how long.
consider: The rate of fading is the judgement, made per class and sometimes per pupil. The strand prose says scaffolds are removed as competence grows, and competence is judged in the room.
Fading the visible scaffold pairs with fading your own live support; the template is one strand of a wider handover.
pages.wider: Rosenshine's principles put scaffolding and its removal at the heart of instruction, and Sweller's load theory explains why the removal has to be gradual.

why: Some things resist the classroom: too fast, too slow, too dangerous, too large. The EEF found simulations let students manipulate variables and see consequences beyond those physical limits.
The card's caveat is the strategy's spine: use a simulation to extend your explanation, not to replace it. Technology serves pedagogy, here as everywhere in the strand.
example: After teaching resistance directly, a physics class opens a circuit simulation and changes one variable at a time, watching the current respond in ways the bench equipment cannot safely or visibly show. The explanation came first; the simulation stretches it.
pages.try: Identify one topic where the real phenomenon cannot come into your room, and check whether the approved tools in your setting include a simulation that could extend your explanation of it.
notice: Whether pupils connect what the simulation shows to the explanation that preceded it, or treat it as a separate game.
The language pupils use afterwards: talk of variables and consequences suggests the manipulation did some work.
consider: A simulation with no explanation around it is a substitution, which is the pattern the EEF's evidence warns against.
Which variables pupils should manipulate, and in what order, is a teaching decision the simulation will not make for you.
tech: Simulation tools and interactive models sit further up the complexity scale than most technology in this strand, which makes the strand's rule more important, not less: pedagogy informs the approach, and the tool enhances and supports. Use the simulation your setting has approved, and use it after the explanation has done its work.
pages.wider: The finding on simulations comes from the EEF's digital technology guidance, the same review behind the strand's supplement-never-substitute rule.

why: A vague aim gives a pupil nothing to steer by. "Do your best on question three" cannot be monitored against, which is why Zimmerman puts a specific, proximal goal at the very start of the self-regulation cycle: learners look ahead before they act.
Asking pupils to state what a good answer to this question looks like, before they start writing it, turns the aim into something they can check their work against while the work is still happening.
example: Before a history essay, pupils jot down three things a strong answer to this exact question would contain. The class compares suggestions, agrees a shared version, and it stays on screen while they write. A pupil who pauses mid-paragraph now has something concrete to pause against.
pages.try: Before your next extended answer, ask "what would a good answer to this include?" and take suggestions before anyone writes a word. Two minutes, no preparation.
notice: Whether the goals pupils state are specific, or just the task restated. "Write a good essay" is the vague aim wearing a costume.
Whether anyone refers back to the goal mid-task. A goal set and then ignored has not yet entered the cycle.
Whether the stated goal changes what gets written.
consider: Pupils new to this will produce woolly criteria at first. That is a reason to model the move, not to abandon it.
The long-term aim is pupils who set the goal without being asked. The prompt is scaffolding, and scaffolding is for fading.
pages.wider: Goal-setting sits in the forethought phase of Zimmerman's self-regulation cycle; the looking ahead is what makes the later monitoring and self-judgement possible.

why: There is a tempting version of metacognition in which pupils are taught to plan, monitor and reflect as a free-standing skill. Willingham's point cuts through it: you cannot plan or monitor a task you know nothing about. A pupil cannot judge whether their circuit explanation is going wrong if they do not know the circuit rules.
So the sequencing matters. Teach the content first; metacognition works on knowledge, never instead of it.
example: Before a science extended task that asks pupils to plan and self-check their approach, the teacher runs a short retrieval starter on the underlying content. Pupils who cannot yet retrieve the basics get more practice on those before the planning and monitoring steps are asked of them; regulation is pointed only at material that exists to be regulated.
pages.try: Put a retrieval starter in front of your next task that demands planning or self-checking, and let the results tell you who is ready to regulate and who still needs the content.
notice: Pupils whose reflections are vague or generic. Often the gap is knowledge, not reflective skill.
Whether the quality of pupils' plans tracks how secure their content is. It usually does, which is the card's argument in miniature.
consider: This cuts against bolt-on study skills lessons taught apart from subjects. Build the base, then regulate, and do both inside the topic.
pages.wider: Willingham's wider argument is that thinking skills depend on knowledge of the thing being thought about; the same warning against teaching metacognition in the abstract runs through the strand's evidence base.

why: The first minute of a task is often spent writing, which is the problem. Zimmerman found that strong learners break a task into its demands before starting; weaker ones answer the question they assumed they were asked, and find out at marking time.
Two questions do most of the work here: what is this question really asking, and which prior topics does it draw on? Both come before the first line goes down.
example: A worded maths problem goes up on the board. Before anyone solves it, the class annotates it together: the quantity actually being asked for is circled, the topics it draws on are named at the side, and the step most likely to catch people out gets a warning mark. Only then do pupils attempt it, and the annotation stays visible.
notice: Pupils who start writing the moment the task lands. Speed of starting is not a good sign here.
Whether the demands pupils identify match the ones you had in mind. The mismatches tell you what to model next.
Misreadings surfacing during analysis rather than in your marking pile. That is the strategy doing its job.
consider: Model the analysis aloud before expecting pupils to do it; the questions look obvious to an expert precisely because the expert no longer notices asking them.
It costs a few minutes at the start of the task. Budget for them, because they are usually repaid at the end.
pages.wider: Task analysis is the opening move of Zimmerman's forethought phase: the reading of demands that everything downstream, goal, strategy and monitoring, depends on.

why: Most pupils do not choose a method; they reach for the first one that comes to mind, or the one they always use. Flavell's point is that planning means selecting an approach, not defaulting to one, and selection only happens when there is a moment of deliberate choice.
Having pupils name which method they will use for this problem, and why, before the first line goes down makes that choice visible, to them and to you.
example: A pair of simultaneous equations goes up, alongside a short menu of the methods the class has been taught: substitution, elimination, graphing. Each pupil writes the method they will use and one line of reasoning in the margin before starting. The teacher scans the reasons, not just the choices; "the coefficients already match" is a different answer from "it's the one I like".
pages.try: On the next task with more than one viable route, ask for the method and the why in the margin before anyone starts. It costs thirty seconds.
notice: Pupils who pick the same method every time regardless of the problem. Habit is wearing planning's clothes.
Whether the stated reasons mention features of the task. Reasons that do are conditional knowledge forming.
consider: Pupils can only select from strategies they have actually been taught. If the menu is empty, teach the methods first and come back to this.
The why matters more than the choice; a defensible reason for the "wrong" method is better planning than a lucky default.
pages.wider: Flavell's metacognitive knowledge includes knowing one's strategies; Winne adds the conditional layer, knowing which one this task calls for.

why: Confidence built on pep talks does not survive contact with a hard task. Zimmerman's finding is that self-efficacy drives effort, but it has to be earned by past success rather than asserted over it.

Pointing a pupil to a recent task they genuinely mastered sets a credible expectation for the one in front of them: not "you can do anything" but "you did something like this three weeks ago, and here it is".
example: Before a demanding analysis essay, pupils reopen a marked piece from earlier in the term where they handled a similar demand well. Each names one thing they did then, a planning move, a way of using evidence, that applies now. The expectation for the new task is anchored to something that actually happened.
pages.try: Before the next task your class will find daunting, name one specific success they have already earned and say exactly why it is relevant. Specific and true, or it does not work.
notice: Whether reluctant starters begin sooner when the anchor is in front of them.
Whether pupils can say what made the earlier success happen. "I worked hard" is a start; a named method is better, and connects to how they explain results.
consider: The reference has to be genuine. A hollow example reads as a pep talk, and the card is explicit that pep talks are not where efficacy comes from.
For a pupil with little recent success in your subject, choosing what to anchor to takes care. The teacher knows the class, not a website.
pages.wider: Self-efficacy belongs to Zimmerman's forethought phase: the expectation a learner carries into a task shapes the effort and persistence they bring to it.

why: Feeling that you understand something is not evidence that you do. Winne showed that a novice's sense of understanding is unreliable, and it is least reliable exactly when it feels strongest, after re-reading familiar material.
The fix is structural rather than motivational: pair every self-check with an external test, a quiz or a worked answer, so monitoring rests on evidence rather than confidence.
example: At the end of a topic segment, pupils rate how secure they feel on it, then immediately take a five-question quiz. The two results sit side by side. For some pupils they agree; for others the quiz disagrees with the feeling, and that disagreement is the most useful thing the lesson produces.
pages.try: Next time you hear yourself ask "are we happy with this?", follow it with three quick questions and let the answers reply.
notice: Pupils who were confident and wrong. They are the reason the external check exists.
Whether pupils start asking for the check themselves. That is the habit beginning to internalise.
consider: Keep the checks low-stakes. The point is calibration, not judgement, and stakes distort both.
The check has to feed action; a gap discovered and then ignored has only decorated the lesson.
tech: A self-marking quiz in your setting's approved tool returns the evidence while the feeling of understanding is still fresh, which is when the comparison teaches most. Be clear about the division of labour: the tool supplies the evidence, and the pupil still does the judging of what it means and what to do next. That part is not for automating.
pages.wider: Winne's model of self-regulated learning puts flawed self-monitoring at its centre: learners regulate on the basis of what they believe about their progress, so the beliefs need correcting by evidence.

why: Monitoring your own attention is itself a skill, and Zimmerman's point is that it develops best in a low-distraction environment first. A pupil cannot practise noticing their focus slipping while twelve tabs are competing for it.

So the environment is scaffolded to begin with, and the scaffold is withdrawn as pupils show they can manage attention themselves. If the restriction never lifts, the tool is doing the regulating and the capacity never gets built.
example: During on-screen independent work, the teacher uses the school's classroom management tool to limit what is open for the first few weeks of the routine. As pupils show they can hold focus, the limits are relaxed, class by class or pupil by pupil, until managing the screen is their job rather than the software's.
pages.try: Before you switch any restriction on, decide what the first step of switching it off will look like, and what evidence would trigger it.
notice: What happens when a restriction lifts. That first unrestricted session tells you whether focus was being learned or merely enforced.
Pupils who work only while they know the tool is active. That is the dependency the fading is designed to avoid.
consider: The fading is the strategy. A monitoring tool used permanently removes the very work that builds the capacity; a guide that hands you the answer makes you dependent on the guide.
When to fade, and for whom, is a judgement call. The teacher knows the class, not a website.
tech: The card names a classroom management tool; use whichever one is approved in your setting, and hold it to the strand's rule: scaffold the regulation, then fade the scaffold. The goal is a learner who no longer needs the tool.
pages.wider: Structuring the environment is one of the self-regulatory strategies Zimmerman documented in the performance phase; the handover from external structure to self-management is where the learning sits.

why: Left alone, monitoring fades. Winne's observation is that pupils absorbed in a task stop checking whether the approach is still working, and the longer they go, the harder a wrong method is to abandon, because sunk effort argues for carrying on.
Planned pauses interrupt that drift. A stop point is a scheduled moment where the question "is this still working?" gets asked whether or not anyone felt like asking it.
example: Fifteen minutes into an extended writing task, a timer marks the stop point. Everyone pauses and answers one question: is my approach still working, and how do I know? A pupil whose structure has drifted from the question notices now, with half the time left, rather than at the end with none.
pages.try: Add one timed pause to the longest task you set this week, with the question written on the board so pupils hit it rather than skip it.
notice: Whether anyone actually changes course at a stop point. Pauses that never alter behaviour are not yet monitoring.
Answers that become pro forma. "Yes, fine" written in four seconds means the check has become a ritual, and rituals need refreshing.
consider: Too many stop points become noise and interrupt the very concentration they are meant to protect. One or two per task, placed where a wrong turn would be costly.
The external prompt carries the remembering-to-check, so pupils' attention can stay on the work itself. That load-carrying is exactly why the prompt can later be faded rather than kept forever.
pages.wider: Winne's contribution to the strand is precisely this: regulation happens while the work is happening, not just after it is finished, and it needs prompting until it becomes habit.

why: Pupils usually discover they did not understand something when the work comes back marked, which is the most expensive possible moment to find out. Monitoring during the task, do I actually understand this, surfaces the gap while there is still time to do something about it.
The question sounds trivial. The habit is not, because self-regulation has to be taught, modelled and practised rather than picked up from being told to reflect.
example: Before an extended task, a teacher plants two checkpoints in it. At each one, pupils stop and answer in the margin: am I sure about what I have just done, or am I guessing? A pupil who writes guessing at checkpoint one has saved twenty minutes of confidently wrong work.
pages.try: Plant one checkpoint in one task this week, with the question written where pupils will hit it. Asking them to answer it in writing, even one word, stops the check being skipped.
notice: Pupils who answer yes and are wrong. A novice's sense of understanding is unreliable, which is why this pairs with an external check rather than replacing one.
Whether anyone changes course after a checkpoint. Monitoring that never alters behaviour is not yet doing its job.
consider: There must be something to monitor. Metacognition works on knowledge, never instead of it, so the content has to be taught before the checking of it can mean anything.
The prompts are scaffolding, and scaffolding is for fading. The long term aim is pupils who ask the question without the checkpoint.
pages.wider: Flavell gave us the language of metacognition; Winne showed why the monitoring has to happen while the work is happening, not just after it is finished.

why: Regulation you cannot see, you cannot coach. A finished product tells you whether a pupil got there; it says almost nothing about the route, and the route is where regulation lives or fails.
Flavell's work is the ground here: pupils can become more aware of their own thinking, and a brief written trace of reasoning is that awareness made inspectable, by you and by them.
example: Working through a multi-step maths problem, pupils add a one-line note at each step saying why they took it. Reviewing the traces, the teacher finds a pupil whose method is sound but aimed at the wrong quantity from step one. The product was wrong; the trace shows exactly which part of the process was not.
pages.try: Ask for a single margin note on the next problem: "why I chose this step". One line is enough to start.
notice: The mismatches: tidy products built on shaky reasoning, and rough products built on sound reasoning. Both are invisible without the trace.
Traces written after the fact to justify the answer. Post-hoc rationalisation is a different activity from showing your working.
consider: Keep the trace brief. If writing about the thinking starts competing with the thinking, the scaffold has become the task.
The trace is for inspection and coaching, not for marking. Announce that, or pupils will write for the grade.
tech: A shared document in your setting's approved platform lets the trace accumulate where you can see it during the task, rather than after the books close. That is invisible thinking made visible while there is still time to act on it; the document shows the process, and the coaching of it remains yours.
pages.wider: Flavell gave us the language for pupils' awareness of their own thinking; the trace turns that awareness into something a teacher can actually work with.

why: Asked to check their work, most pupils check how it feels, and "it feels done" wins. Zimmerman's point is that self-judgement needs a reference, not a hunch: evaluation without a standard is just mood.
Giving pupils the mark scheme or an exemplar to compare against turns "is it good?" into "does it do what this does?", which is a question they can actually answer.
example: Pupils lay their own paragraph beside an exemplar, with the mark scheme between them, and identify one criterion their work meets and one it misses. The judgement is a comparison with something real, and the missed criterion becomes the obvious next move.
pages.try: In your next self-assessment moment, replace "check your work" with "compare your work to this", and put the this in front of them.
notice: Whether pupils' judgements of their own work drift closer to yours over time. Calibration against a standard is learnable.
Pupils who can recite the criteria but cannot find them in their own writing. Reading an exemplar is itself a skill to teach.
consider: Choose the exemplar to show the standard, not perfection. Work just above the pupil's current level gives the comparison something to grip.
This pairs naturally with goals set before the task; the standard used at the end means more when it was in view at the start.
pages.wider: Zimmerman's self-reflection phase turns on comparing performance against a standard; this strategy simply makes sure the standard is real and present rather than imagined.

why: What a pupil says to themselves after a result shapes what they do with the next one. Zimmerman's finding is that attribution feeds forward: a result explained by fixed ability, "I'm just bad at maths", closes the conversation, because ability cannot be changed by Tuesday.
A result explained by method stays open. The method used can be named, examined and altered, which is why attribution is steered towards it.
example: When an assessment comes back, the reflection prompt asks: which part of how you prepared helped most, and what would you change about how you prepare next time? A pupil who writes "self-quizzing worked, I left the second topic too late" has produced something usable. "I'm not a science person" would have produced nothing.
pages.try: Change the question you ask after results, in your written comments first. Method questions model method attributions.
notice: The language pupils reach for unprompted after results. Ability talk and method talk are easy to tell apart once you listen for them.
Whether a changed explanation changes the next preparation. Attribution is only doing its work when it feeds forward.
consider: Your own feedback language carries most of the weight here; praise aimed at the strategy rather than the person is this card operating in your marking.
Method attributions have to be true. If the preparation was genuinely fine and the paper was brutal, say so; honesty is what keeps the reflection worth doing.
pages.wider: In Zimmerman's cycle the self-reflection phase feeds the next forethought phase; attributions are the hinge between the two, which is why they are worth steering.

why: A great deal of classroom reflection ends at the reflection. "I should be more careful" is written, the book closes, and nothing is different on Monday. Butler's point is exact: feedback only regulates learning if it changes the next action.
So each reflection gets converted into one concrete adjustment, named and attached to the very next task. Reflection only earns the name metacognition when it changes what the learner does next.
example: After a marked assessment, each pupil writes a single line in an action log: next time I will plan for five minutes before writing, or next time I will check units before moving on. The log travels forward, and it is open on the desk at the start of the next comparable task, where the promise meets its moment.
pages.try: End your next reflection activity one step later than usual: not "what went wrong?" but "what will you do differently on the next one, specifically?"
notice: Adjustments that are checkable versus adjustments that are wishes. "Try harder" cannot be verified; "plan for five minutes first" can.
Whether the log actually gets consulted when the next task arrives. An action log nobody reopens is a reflection graveyard.
The same adjustment appearing twice. That repeat is telling you the loop has not closed.
consider: One adjustment, not five. A single specific change can actually be made and actually be checked.
The gap matters: the next comparable task needs to arrive while the plan is still warm. Sequencing tasks so that it does is your end of the bargain.
pages.wider: Butler's model treats self-regulation and feedback as one loop: what a learner notices about their work matters only insofar as it alters the next attempt.

why: Pupils are usually most confident about the material they met most recently, not the material they actually know. That miscalibration drives bad revision decisions all the way to the exam hall.
Prediction makes calibration visible. Write the score you expect, see the score you got, and the gap between the two becomes evidence a pupil can learn from, week on week.
example: Before handing in a low-stakes quiz, every pupil writes a predicted score in the corner. When the quizzes come back, they log predicted against actual and note the direction they missed in. After four quizzes, one pupil can see he always overestimates on definitions and underestimates on application, which quietly rewrites his revision plan.
pages.try: Add the predicted-score corner to your next low-stakes quiz. The comparison takes one minute when the quiz is returned, and the value builds over repetitions rather than arriving in week one.
notice: The direction of error, which matters more than its size. Systematic overconfidence and systematic underconfidence need different conversations.
Whether gaps narrow over time. The card's phrase is the goal: monitoring corrected by evidence.
consider: Keep the stakes low. The moment a prediction affects anything that counts, pupils manage the prediction instead of learning from it.
This works best attached to a regular quizzing routine that already exists, rather than as a reason to invent one.
pages.wider: Winne's work on calibration sits behind this, alongside Dunlosky and Metcalfe's finding that confidence tracks recency rather than knowledge; the strand's further reading takes both further.

why: Reflection is usually treated as the pupil's business: they notice their errors, they act on them. Butler's insight is that self-regulation and instruction are a loop, and the teacher is inside it. What pupils notice about their own errors is evidence you can plan from.
It also changes how pupils treat reflection. When Monday's lesson visibly begins from what they reported on Friday, reporting honestly starts to have a point.
example: At the end of the lesson, an exit poll asks each pupil to name the error they made most, or the step they felt least sure of. The teacher tallies the responses, and the next lesson opens by reteaching the most common one, saying so out loud: most of you said the same thing, so we start there.
pages.try: One exit question this week: "which part are you least sure of?" Then act on the tally where the class can see you doing it.
notice: Whether what pupils report matches the errors actually in their work. When it does not, that mismatch is your next teaching point about self-monitoring.
Whether self-diagnosis gets sharper once pupils see their reports being used. Consequences tend to improve the reporting.
consider: The visible acting-on is what makes this work; collected reflections that vanish teach pupils that reflection is paperwork.
Where reports and work disagree, the reflection is still useful, just differently: it tells you the monitoring needs teaching, not only the content.
pages.wider: Butler frames instruction and self-regulation as a single loop rather than parallel tracks; this strategy is that loop run deliberately, with the teacher's next move as its output.

why: "Go and revise" assumes pupils own methods to revise with. Many do not, which is Flavell's point: students cannot deploy a strategy they have never been taught. What fills the gap is usually re-reading and highlighting, because those need no instruction.
Retrieval, spacing and self-explanation have to be taught explicitly, as named methods with steps, before independent use can reasonably be expected.
example: A teacher spends part of a lesson teaching self-quizzing as a method in its own right: what it is called, how to build questions from notes, how to check answers honestly. The class practises it together on current content, the steps go onto a reference sheet, and only after guided practice does it appear in homework instructions by name.
pages.try: Pick one strategy your instructions currently assume, and teach it explicitly this half term: name, steps, practice, the lot.
notice: Whether pupils use the method's name themselves. Named strategies get chosen; vague ones dissolve back into re-reading.
What revision actually looks like when you ask pupils to show you rather than tell you. The gap between claimed and real methods is usually instructive.
consider: Explicit teaching, then guided practice, then independence, in that order. Expecting the third without the first two is where "go and revise" fails.
Teach the strategy inside the content it serves rather than in the abstract; a method learned on real material travels better into use.
pages.wider: Flavell counted knowledge of strategies among the foundations of metacognition; the EEF's guidance draws the same line, putting explicit strategy instruction before independent use.

why: Owning a strategy is not the same as knowing when to reach for it. Winne calls this conditional knowledge, and argues it is what separates skilled learners: not a bigger toolbox, but a better sense of which tool this task calls for.
That means teaching the cues, the features of a task that signal which method fits, and not just the methods themselves.
example: The teacher shows two worked cases side by side: a vocabulary-heavy topic matched to flashcards and spaced review, and an essay question matched to planning plus self-explanation. The question to the class is not "what are these methods?" but "what was it about each task that made that the right match?"
pages.try: Next time you name a strategy in class, add the when: the one or two task features that make it the right call here.
notice: Pupils' answers to "why this method for this task?". Feature-based answers are conditional knowledge arriving.
Strategies misapplied with full confidence, flashcards aimed at essay skills, say. The method is fine; the matching is the gap.
consider: Conditional knowledge grows from comparing cases, so one example is not enough; contrast is what makes the cues visible.
If your class keeps a strategy reference sheet, add a when column to it. The cue belongs next to the method.
pages.wider: Winne's account of self-regulated learning gives conditional knowledge, knowing which strategy suits which conditions, the deciding role in whether regulation actually helps.

why: A scaffold that never comes down has become part of the building. Zimmerman's point is blunt: support must be withdrawn for self-regulation to develop, because a pupil who is always prompted to plan, check and reflect never has to remember to.

The route runs from modelled to guided to independent use, with prompts removed as pupils show they no longer need them. Self-regulation has to be taught, modelled, practised and gradually handed over; this card is the handing over.
example: Essay planning prompts follow a planned retreat across the year: a full prompt sheet modelled and used in the autumn, a shortened cue card in the spring, and by summer a blank page, with the cue card still available to the pupils whose work shows they need it.
pages.try: Choose one prompt that has become permanent furniture in your classroom, and decide what evidence would tell you it can start to fade.
notice: What happens on the first unprompted task. That is the honest measure of whether the scaffold was teaching or substituting.
Pupils still receiving prompts they demonstrably no longer need. Fading late has costs too; the support becomes a ceiling.
consider: Fade by readiness, not by calendar, and not necessarily whole-class. Who is ready is a judgement only the teacher in the room can make.
Fading is not final. A pupil who struggles without the prompt gets it back, and the fade restarts from there.
pages.wider: Zimmerman traced the development of self-regulation from observing a model through to independent use; the strand's whole argument about tools and prompts, scaffold then fade, is that trajectory applied.

why: Pupils keep study methods the way anyone keeps habits: because they are familiar and feel productive, not because they have checked. Re-reading survives on exactly this. Winne's finding is that learners refine an approach by checking whether it worked, which means the checking has to be arranged.
Trial a method, judge it against results, keep only what the evidence supports. It is the scientific method pointed at your own studying.
example: For three weeks, pupils log one line before each weekly quiz: which method they used to prepare. Afterwards they add the score. At the end they read their own log: one pupil finds the evenings spent recopying notes tracked with their lowest scores, and the ten-minute self-quiz with their highest. The log makes the case; the teacher does not have to.
pages.try: Attach a one-line method log to a quiz routine you already run. The infrastructure exists; only the logging is new.
notice: Comfort methods that the log shows underperforming. Watching a pupil meet that evidence is the strategy at work.
Whether anyone actually drops a method. Keeping the winner is easy; dropping the familiar loser is the hard part, and the part worth praising.
consider: This needs a regular assessment rhythm to judge against; without one, there is no evidence for the log to collect.
Single data points mislead, so judge across weeks, not after one quiz. A method is not condemned by one bad Friday.
pages.wider: Winne describes self-regulated learners as running a feedback loop over their own methods, evaluating each against outcomes and updating; this strategy builds that loop where pupils can see it.

why: A strategy taught in the abstract tends to stay there. Willingham's argument is that strategies do not float free of subjects: self-regulating an essay is not the same act as self-regulating a proof, and pupils taught "metacognition" in general often cannot find it again inside geography.
So each strategy is taught inside the content it serves. Pupils learn to self-regulate this topic, in this subject, and the strategy arrives already attached to somewhere it works.
example: Rather than sending the class to a generic study skills session, the geography teacher teaches self-quizzing inside the rivers topic, using rivers vocabulary, and adds it to a subject strategy bank: which methods suit map skills, which suit case studies, which suit extended writing. The strategy and the content are learned as one thing.
pages.try: Take one strategy currently taught generically in your school and re-teach it inside the topic where it pays off most in your subject.
notice: Whether pupils use the strategy in the subject where they learned it but nowhere else. Transfer is genuinely hard; expect to teach the strategy again in new territory rather than assume it travels.
Whether the strategy bank gets consulted, or exists only as a display.
consider: This makes strategy instruction every department's job rather than a discrete course; a subject-specific bank is only credible when the subject's teachers built it.
pages.wider: Willingham has long argued that thinking skills are bound to the content they operate on; the same warning against content-free metacognition runs through the strand's evidence base.

why: Spacing is usually something done to pupils: the teacher builds the retrieval schedule and the pupils turn up to it. That works, but it leaves the regulation with the teacher. Deciding when you will study is a planning act, and it can be handed over.
Teaching pupils to set their own calendar reminders to revisit topics puts the spacing schedule in their hands, which is the point where a classroom routine starts becoming a study habit.
example: At the end of a topic, pupils set three reminders on their calendar: a few days out, a fortnight out, a month out. Each reminder names an action, not a topic: quiz myself on the glossary, redraw the diagram from memory. When it fires, the review is ten minutes, and it is retrieval rather than re-reading.
pages.try: Do it together in class the first time, and check the wording of each reminder names something to do, not something to look at.
notice: Whether reminders name actions or just topics. "Revise photosynthesis" fires and gets dismissed; "self-quiz on the photosynthesis flashcards" fires and gets done more often.
Whether pupils set their own reminders for later topics without being told. Unprompted scheduling is the handover happening.
What actually occurs when a reminder fires. Ask; the answer tells you whether the system is real.
consider: The reminder is the trigger; the review it triggers must be retrieval, or the schedule is just spaced re-reading.
Start with a class-set schedule and fade towards pupil-set, like any other scaffold in this strand.
pages.wider: Zimmerman would file this under forethought: planning applied to study time itself. The evidence on spacing that it draws on sits with the retrieval practice strand.

why: Writing a good question is harder than answering one, and that is the value. To build a quiz from your own notes you must judge which ideas carry the topic, what is likely to be asked, and what a fair test of it looks like: monitoring decisions, all of them.
The tool then supports retrieval the pupil has authored, rather than serving up someone else's judgement of what counts.
example: Pupils turn their notes on a topic into ten flashcards. The constraint does the teaching: each card front must be answerable without giving the answer away, which forces decisions about what the essential knowledge actually is. The finished deck then drives their retrieval practice for the weeks that follow.
pages.try: End a topic with "write five questions a classmate should be able to answer", then swap and answer. Authoring and retrieval in one move, no technology required to start.
notice: Questions that only target the easiest facts. That is a judgement gap, and it is teachable: show what a probing question looks like and let them revise their own.
Whether question quality improves once pupils have seen good models.
consider: The authoring is where the thinking happens. A downloaded deck has had all the deciding done already, which is precisely the part the pupil needed to do.
Swapping questions buys a second benefit: answering a peer's questions is another retrieval pass, from a different angle.
tech: A flashcard or low-stakes quiz tool approved in your setting will happily manage the practice: storing the deck, shuffling the order, resurfacing cards over time. What it must not manage is the writing of the questions. Keep the authoring with the pupil and let the tool carry the admin; that division is the strand's rule about scaffolds applied to a quiz app.
pages.wider: Winne's account of self-regulated studying underpins this: deciding what to ask yourself is itself a monitoring judgement, made before a single answer is attempted.

why: The environment a pupil has to regulate now includes the one in their pocket. Managing attention used to mean choosing a seat away from friends; it now also means deciding what the device is allowed to do while you work.

The card's distinction is between imposed and chosen: teaching pupils to switch on focus modes and silence alerts as a deliberate act puts the regulation with them, so the tool serves attention instead of stealing it.
example: Independent study begins with a standing routine: before anything else, pupils set their device to focus mode and silence notifications, the same way they get equipment out. The step takes seconds. Over time the teacher stops cueing it, and watches who still does it.
notice: Who reaches for focus mode unprompted once the cueing stops. That is the habit either forming or not.
What pupils say when asked why they do it. A rule being followed and a choice being understood sound different, and only the second survives leaving school.
consider: The deliberate choice is the strategy. A block imposed from above does the regulating for the pupil, which has its place as an early scaffold, but is a different card; this one is the handover.
What pupils can control on school-managed devices varies, so build the routine within your setting's device policy and around the settings pupils genuinely own.
pages.wider: Zimmerman documented environmental structuring as a strategy self-regulated learners use deliberately; the screen is simply the newest environment to structure.

why: Willingham's line is the whole argument: memory is the residue of thought. A pupil who offloads the thinking to AI has done no thinking, so there is no residue; nothing is learned, however polished the work looks.

The distinction the card draws is between AI producing the reasoning and AI challenging reasoning the pupil has already done. The first is substitution and hollows out the very capacity this strand is trying to build. The second can work like an external check, provided the judging of the critique stays with the pupil.
example: A pupil finishes a written argument, then asks the approved AI tool to find the weakest step in their reasoning. The tool points at a paragraph. The pupil now has a decision to make: is the critique right, and if so, what changes? They revise, or they reject the critique with a reason. Either way, the reasoning, both rounds of it, was theirs.
pages.try: Trial it on work that is already finished, so the only thing the tool can touch is the checking. The order, thinking first and tool second, is the whole safeguard.
notice: Pupils who accept the critique wholesale. Offloading judgement to the critic is offloading too, just one step later.
Whether revisions show the pupil's own reasoning about the critique, or just compliance with it.
What the work looks like when the tool is not available. That is the residue check.
consider: This sits inside your setting's policy on pupil AI use; where pupils cannot use such tools directly, the same critique step works with a peer or a mark scheme instead.
A pupil with nothing yet on the page has nothing for a critic to work on. The card's sequence is not optional.
tech: Used within the card's framing, as a critic of work the pupil has already produced, an approved AI tool in your setting can supply the external challenge that self-monitoring needs. The moment it drafts, plans or fixes on the pupil's behalf, it is doing the regulating, and a guide that hands you the answer makes you dependent on the guide. Scaffold the regulation, then fade the scaffold; the goal here, as everywhere in this strand, is a learner who no longer needs the tool.
pages.wider: Willingham's memory-as-residue-of-thought principle does the heavy lifting: whatever the pupil does not think about, the pupil does not learn, whoever or whatever did the thinking instead.
